title: PyPI trusted-publishing upload is gated in source only by writer-editable workflow logic; whether a writer without release authority can publish depends on unobserved `pypi` environment, tag and PyPI publisher settings
description: publish.yml uploads to PyPI with OIDC trusted publishing whenever a GitHub release is published (publish.yml:13-16, 86-92, 130-131). The only gate visible in source is scripts/check_release_tag.py. It compares the tag string with the [project] version in the checked-out pyproject.toml, and nothing else (check_release_tag.py:36-39). It reads no git state, so it cannot check the tagged commit's ancestry, signer or creator. Nothing in the workflow binds the tagged commit to main, although release.md:133 says the release creates the tag on main. Take a principal who has write access but no release authority: a collaborator, an installed app, or a stolen writer token. On GitHub the write role can create releases. That principal could push a side branch whose code is modified and whose version line matches, then publish a release on a tag pointing at that branch. The workflow would check out the tag's commit, pass the tag check, build it, and upload it as vfs-py. The `if: github.event_name == 'release'` guard on the publish job (publish.yml:87) and the tag-check steps are read from the workflow file at the triggering ref, so a writer also controls them on their own branch. Only hosted controls decide whether the upload can happen: protection rules on the `pypi` environment (required reviewers, deployment branch and tag policy), tag rulesets for v*, branch protection on main, the collaborator and app list, and the PyPI trusted-publisher record. None of these is in source. The repository does not record them either: the roadmap audit (07-release-ci-and-repo-hygiene.md:106) and spec 166 criterion 12 list the trusted-publisher check as a pending item, and release.md has no such note yet. Fork and PR contributors cannot reach this path. publish.yml has no pull_request, pull_request_target or workflow_run trigger, and both releasing and dispatching need write access. The prior code review (2026-11-06-the-release-lane-to-0-1-0-code-review.md:73-75) also found no lower-trust principal below a repository writer. Whether any writer who lacks release authority exists is the deciding fact.
claimed_root_cause: Inside the workflow, the release's source identity (the tagged commit and the triggering ref) is never bound to reviewed main. The only in-source gate is a string comparison between the tag and the version, and it reads only pyproject.toml. The `pypi` environment's protection rules and the PyPI trusted-publisher record are the only controls that could bind the release to a release owner and an approved ref, and neither is in source.

trace.description: Anyone who can publish a release, or dispatch the workflow on any ref, starts the run. Both need write access. Neither event is restricted to main or to a tag pattern in source.
actions/checkout with no ref checks out GITHUB_SHA: the release tag's commit, or the dispatched ref. That commit need not be reachable from main.
Runs scripts/check_release_tag.py "$TAG", with the tag passed through env and quoted. This is the only source gate before the build and the upload.
Returns 0 when tag == 'v' + the version in the checked-out pyproject.toml. It reads no git state: no ancestry from main, no signer, no tag creator.
Builds the wheels, and at :76 the sdist, from the checked-out commit's code.

Runs with `if: github.event_name == 'release'`, environment pypi and permission id-token: write. The guard comes from the workflow file at the triggering ref, which a writer can edit on their own branch.
`uv publish --trusted-publishing always` mints a PyPI upload token from the job's OIDC identity and uploads dist/ as vfs-py.

evidence.description: States the intended policy: the GitHub release creates the vX.Y.Z tag on main. The workflow does not enforce it.
'The workflow runs no tests. It trusts main is green.' The publish path assumes its source is main and never checks it. The tag check is named as its only gate.
`environment: pypi` is the only hook for a hosted approval or a deployment-ref policy. Its protection rules are not in source.

A pending roadmap item, not a record: trusted publishing is still to be confirmed for ClayGendron/vfs, publish.yml and environment pypi. Spec 166 criterion 12 (context/specifications/archive/166-the-release-lane-to-0-1-0/spec.md:177) has the same status, and release.md does not carry the note yet. Even when it is configured, a PyPI trusted-publisher record names the repository, the workflow file and, optionally, the environment. It does not name a git ref, so the environment's own rules decide.
The check is string equality between the tag and the version. The script reads only pyproject.toml (lines 24-27, 36).
The prior review found no lower-trust principal below a repository writer. This agrees with the candidate: the finding is reachable only if some writer lacks release authority.

blockers: The protection rules of the GitHub environment `pypi` cannot be seen from source: required reviewers, whether admins can bypass them, and the policy for deployment branches and tags (for example, only tags matching v*, or only main).

It cannot be seen whether a ruleset limits creating, updating or deleting tags matching v* to release owners, or whether branch protection on main stops a writer from pushing straight to main. Without branch protection, binding the release to main would not be enough on its own.

The list of collaborators, teams and installed apps cannot be seen, so neither can whether any principal with write access but no release authority exists. If Clay is the only writer and no app has write access, no lower-trust principal exists and the candidate is hardening only.

It cannot be seen whether the PyPI trusted publisher for vfs-py exists and names environment `pypi`. The repository records this only as a pending item. Without the environment binding, any job in publish.yml on any ref, including one that skips the environment, could mint an upload token.

validation_plan.local: Optional, and it shows only the source half. In a harmless fixture under scratch, with no network, write a pyproject.toml whose [project] version is 9.9.9a1. Run `./.venv/bin/python -I scripts/check_release_tag.py v9.9.9a1 --pyproject <fixture>/pyproject.toml` under tools/sandbox-run.py and expect exit 0. The script reads no git state (check_release_tag.py:24-39), so the commit's position in the graph cannot change the result, and reading the source already establishes this. The hosted half needs the owner checks.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed only. Make no release, tag, dispatch or upload. (1) Settings > Environments > pypi: confirm that Required reviewers lists only release owners, that admin bypass is off, and that 'Deployment branches and tags' is restricted, for example to tags matching v*, backed by a tag ruleset. (2) Settings > Rules: confirm that a tag ruleset limits creating, updating and deleting v* tags to release owners, and that main has branch protection or a ruleset requiring review. (3) Settings > Collaborators and teams, and Settings > GitHub Apps: list every principal with write, maintain or admin access, or with release-creation permission. (4) PyPI vfs-py > Settings > Publishing: confirm that the trusted publisher names owner ClayGendron, repository vfs, workflow publish.yml and environment pypi, and that no other publisher or long-lived API token exists. Close the candidate as hardening if (3) shows no writer without release authority, or if (1) has required reviewers limited to release owners and (4) names the environment. Otherwise any such writer can reach the upload. Source defence in depth: on the release event, have the publish job check out with fetch-depth: 0 and fail unless `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$GITHUB_SHA" origin/main` succeeds. Add this on top of the environment deployment rule that limits deployments to v* tags, not in place of it.

title: grant() and revoke() are checked only at the addressed path, so a caller that gets read_write from the everyone posture at an ancestor can grant itself (or anyone) access to a private posture hole beneath it, or revoke others' access there
description: Before a grant or a revoke, the gate checks one thing: does the caller hold read_write at the exact path it named? That check counts read_write the caller gets from the everyone level (the posture). A grant row, though, covers the path and its whole subtree. Grant rows only add access, and a principal's covering row outranks any deeper, narrower posture. Take a mount whose ancestor posture gives everyone read_write (the default for a fresh DatabaseStorage/InMemoryStorage) and whose child folder has a narrower posture such as none. That is the 'open root with a private child' shape. On it, any named principal with no rows can grant itself read (or read_write) at the ancestor, then read and overwrite the private child and re-posture it open to everyone. An anonymous router caller can do the same by granting to a principal it names. A revoke at the ancestor likewise strips another principal's access inside the hole, which the revoker could not see. The caller held nothing in that child. delete/move/sweep run a subtree check (WriteGate.subtrees) that catches this posture hole. grant and revoke do not.
root_cause: _grant_refusal (src/vfs/storage/backends/database/rights.py:1305-1336) reads posture rows only for ancestors_and_self(path) (line 1327). It allows the call as soon as gate.resolution.at('read_write').reaches(path, label) is true (line 1332). Rights.reaches (src/vfs/storage/grants.py:477-479) is a point test: everyone_level >= need at the path itself, or the caller's spans cover that one path. It never asks whether the caller holds the level across the subtree the new row will cover, although Rights.covers_subtree (grants.py:481) exists for exactly that. grant_rows then upserts a principal row at path (rights.py:919). Rights.admits (grants.py:493) returns True on covers(path) for every row beneath that prefix, holes included, so the new row overrides the deeper posture. revoke_rows uses the same point gate, so it can delete a row whose effect reaches into a hole.
intended_behavior: Spec 058 section 8 (context/specifications/archive/058-row-level-permission-grants/spec.md:74) says the granting subject set must hold read_write on the path and 'may grant at most its own level (attenuation)'. The router docstring (src/vfs/base.py:1614-1615) says 'so nobody grants more than it holds'. The grant_rows docstring (rights.py:909-910) says 'what it grants never exceeds its own level there'. Spec 058 section 6 (spec.md:64) requires subtree mutations to check beneath the target 'since an owner-floor row or a posture hole can sit inside a writable directory'. A grant or revoke at /P should be refused unless the granter holds the required level throughout /P's subtree: either its own spans cover the subtree, or no posture row beneath /P gives everyone less than that level at a prefix the spans do not cover.

trace.description: Public grant verb taking path, principal and level from the caller. With no authority it acts as default_authority or anonymous (base.py:3094-3107). revoke follows the same route.
Applies only the mount permission layers via _gate_entry for the addressed rel path, then dispatches to the storage grant verb (line 2044).
Bumps the revision, resolves the gate at VERB_RUNGS[op] = read_write (line 1595), and runs grant_rows or revoke_rows.
Reads posture rows only for ancestors_and_self(path) and computes the everyone label at the addressed path. Posture rows beneath the path are never read.
Returns None (allowed) when gate.resolution.at('read_write').reaches(path, label). An everyone read_write at the path is enough.
Point test: everyone_level >= need or self.covers(path). It does not test the subtree; covers_subtree at line 481 does, and WriteGate.subtrees uses it, but the grant gate does not.

Writes (principal, path, level). Rights.admits (grants.py:493) then admits every row beneath path through covers(), whatever the deeper posture says. revoke_rows (rights.py:945-950) deletes a row at path under the same point gate.

evidence.description: _grant_refusal is the shared gate for grant, revoke and posture. It judges read_write only at the addressed path.
covers_subtree() exists and is the subtree-aware test, but the grant gate calls only the point test reaches() (line 477).
WriteGate.subtrees is the sibling control. delete/move/sweep use it to refuse when a row beneath the target fails the rung, posture holes included. grant/revoke have no equivalent.
Rights.admits returns True on covers(path), so a principal row at /P admits /P/Q rows even when everyone_level there is 0.
Declared contract: 'so nobody grants more than it holds'.
grant_rows docstring: 'what it grants never exceeds its own level there'.
Spec requires attenuation: the granter 'may grant at most its own level'. grant is not listed among the developer-plane-only verbs, so it is an agent-facing verb.
Subtree mutations must check beneath the target because 'a posture hole can sit inside a writable directory'. The grant verbs are not held to this.
The default posture is read_write, so a mount that only narrows a child posture is exposed with no explicit root posture (reproduced).
test_nobody_grants_more_than_it_holds tests attenuation only at the addressed path. No test grants or revokes at an ancestor of a posture hole.

Independent verifier run (InMemoryStorage, sandboxed). Default root posture, /team/hr posture none: eve is refused reading the hr file (not_found), refused granting at /team/hr (not_found), refused deleting /team (permission_denied). eve grant('/', 'eve', 'read') answers ok, then eve reads 'DUMMY-PRIVATE'. eve grant('/team', 'eve', 'read_write') answers ok, then overwrite ok, re-posture /team/hr read_write ok, and anonymous then reads the file. Router with no authority: anon read is unauthenticated and grant at /team/hr is unauthenticated, but grant('/team', 'eve', 'read') answers ok and eve reads the secret.

Independent revoke run: system grants bob read_write at /team, /team/hr posture none. bob reads hr ok, eve gets not_found. eve revoke('/team', 'bob') answers ok, and bob then gets not_found inside the hole.

conditions.description: An ancestor path P has an everyone level that reaches read_write (the default posture of a fresh DatabaseStorage/InMemoryStorage, or an explicit one), and a deeper posture row at P/Q narrows everyone to less (none, list, read, add or contribute). Spec 058 tests this 'open root with a private child' shape.

Any named Authority with no rows of its own is enough. Through the router, an anonymous call (no authority and no default_authority) is also enough, because unauthenticated_at is judged only at P, where everyone holds read_write. Anonymous cannot name itself as grantee ('anon' is reserved), so it grants to a principal it names or controls.
Protected rows exist beneath P/Q, or are written there later; the grant also covers future rows. For the revoke variant, another principal holds a row at P that gives it access inside P/Q.

execution.attacker_perspective: A named principal 'eve' with no grant rows, or an anonymous caller through AsyncVirtualFileSystem, on a mount with the default read_write posture whose /team/hr posture is none.
payloads: await fs.grant('/team', 'eve', 'read')  # AsyncVirtualFileSystem(storage=...), no authority -> anonymous
instructions: Create InMemoryStorage(). As Authority.system(), write /team/hr/salaries.md (dummy content 'DUMMY-PRIVATE') and /team/notes.md with parents=True. Leave the root at its default posture and set posture('/team/hr', 'none').
As eve, confirm the baseline: read('/team/hr/salaries.md') -> not_found; grant('/team/hr', 'eve', 'read_write') -> not_found; delete('/team') -> permission_denied.
As eve, call grant('/', 'eve', 'read') (or grant('/team', 'eve', 'read_write')). It answers ok.
As eve, read /team/hr/salaries.md (ok, 'DUMMY-PRIVATE'); with the read_write row, overwrite it and set posture('/team/hr', 'read_write'); anonymous can then read it.

Router variant: AsyncVirtualFileSystem(storage=...) with no authority: read -> unauthenticated, grant('/team/hr', ...) -> unauthenticated, grant('/team', 'eve', 'read') -> ok, then eve reads the file.
Revoke variant: system grants bob read_write at /team, then posture('/team/hr', 'none'). eve revoke('/team', 'bob') -> ok; bob's read of the hr file goes from ok to not_found.
Run with tools/sandbox-run.py and .venv/bin/python -I (no network, empty env, scratch-only writes).
execution.observed_result: Verifier run, direct: eve read hr -> vfs.not_found; grant at /team/hr -> vfs.not_found; delete /team -> vfs.permission_denied; grant / eve read -> ok; read hr -> ok 'DUMMY-PRIVATE'; grant /team eve read_write -> ok; overwrite -> ok; posture /team/hr read_write -> ok; anonymous read -> ok. Router, anonymous: read -> vfs.unauthenticated; grant /team/hr -> vfs.unauthenticated; grant /team eve read -> ok; eve read -> ok 'DUMMY-PRIVATE'. Revoke: bob read ok; eve read not_found; eve revoke bob at /team ok; bob read not_found. This matches the hunter's independent observation.

remediation.strategy: Make the grant and revoke gate check the subtree the row covers, not just the addressed point, as WriteGate.subtrees does for delete/move/sweep. When the caller's own spans at the required rung do not cover the subtree (neither rights.whole nor rights.covers_subtree(path)), read the posture ('*') rows strictly beneath path. Read them in bounded pages over the bytewise range (path + '/', path + '0') on grants where principal_id = '*', chunked by the membership budget. Refuse with permission_denied when any of them gives everyone less than the rung at a prefix the caller's spans do not cover whole. Add a contract test on every StorageContract leg: open root, private /P/Q. A principal with no rows, and anonymous through the router, must be refused grant and revoke at /P and at /, and still be allowed at an unrelated open sibling.

likelihood.reason: The attacker needs only an ordinary named Authority, or none at all through the router. The precondition is an operator choice: a narrower posture on a child under a permissive ancestor. That shape is documented and tested, and the default posture already supplies the permissive ancestor.

impact.reason: A principal with no rights in the private subtree gains read or full read_write over it: it reads every row, overwrites or trashes them, and can re-posture the subtree open to everyone, anonymous included. The revoke variant lets it remove other principals' access inside the hole. This crosses the row-rights boundary between anonymous or named callers and protected entries.

confidence.reason: Every trace line was checked in source at 3586750. The verifier reproduced the result independently in a sandboxed InMemoryStorage run, which uses the DatabaseStorage rights code path, both directly and through the router as anonymous, and for revoke. The refused baselines (not_found at the hole, permission_denied on delete) show that the posture hole is meant to be enforced. No other layer checks beneath the grant prefix.

title: markdown_refs folds the whole enclosing line once per reference, so one agent-written single-line markdown body makes reindex hold the mount's writer transaction for quadratic time
description: During reindex, the chunk pass sends every dirty markdown body to the Rust markdown_refs. That function calls line_context once for each link destination or path-shaped code span. line_context scans back to the previous newline and forward to the next one, then folds the whole line, and only after that keeps 256 characters. So a body with N references on one line of length about N costs O(N^2). The parse runs on the offload pool with the GIL released, so the event loop keeps running. But it is awaited inside chunk_dirty's writer transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite; on InMemoryStorage, the single serialized session), and there is no time, size or reference budget on it. Every other principal's write to that mount waits until the parse finishes. In an independent run, one 160 KB single-line file written by alice made the operator's reindex take about 7.0 s, against about 0.6 s for the same bytes and references spread over 16,000 lines. bob's unrelated write waited 6.7 s on InMemoryStorage and 6.9 s on file-backed SQLite. Each doubling of the line costs about 3.7-3.9x. The stall comes back on every reindex after the file is rewritten.
root_cause: line_context (crates/vfs-core/src/links.rs:71-75) recomputes the line bounds with rposition/position over the whole line and calls fold_line over the whole line for every reference. fold_line (links.rs:78-93) builds the full folded copy before it truncates to MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS. The per-reference cost is therefore O(line length), not O(MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS). The quadratic work is reachable while a writer transaction is open: _gram_phases runs chunk_dirty inside _execute_write (backend.py:1375), and chunk_dirty awaits call_offloaded(_assess_and_split) (indexing.py:330). _assess_and_split ends with extract_link_work over every dirty markdown body (indexing.py:583). None of these places has a deadline or a per-body cap.
intended_behavior: Reference extraction should be linear in body size, and each reference's context should cost at most O(MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS). CPU that reindex spends on caller-written content should be bounded, or should run without the mount's writer lock held, so that one principal's document cannot block other principals' writes for superlinear time.

trace.description: A lower-trust named principal (alice) writes a .md body that holds N link destinations on one line. No body-size or line-length cap exists on this path.
The operator's reindex runs chunk_dirty inside _execute_write. That is a BEGIN IMMEDIATE writer transaction on SQLite, and the one serialized session on InMemoryStorage.
call_offloaded(_assess_and_split) is awaited while the writer transaction is open, with no deadline.
extract_link_work(rows, links_generation) runs over every dirty markdown body.
extract_links passes the bodies to native.markdown_refs (models/links.py:78, python.rs:207), which parses each body on one thread, off the GIL.
line_context(body, node.start_byte()) is called once for every link_destination and path-shaped code_span.
rposition and position over the whole line, then fold_line over the whole line, for each reference: O(N x line length) CPU while the writer lock is held.

evidence.description: line_context scans to both ends of the line and folds all of it before the result is cut to MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS.
fold_line iterates every char of the line and builds the whole folded string. Only the final collect takes 256 chars, so there is no early exit.
The offloaded split is awaited inside the writer transaction, with no budget.
_execute_write marks the connection vfs_writer, so SQLite opens BEGIN IMMEDIATE and holds the write lock from the first read.
Other SQLite writers wait up to busy_timeout 5000 ms per attempt. Under with_retry (engine.py:298) they get a bounded number of attempts and then a conflict.
On InMemoryStorage, _SerializedSessions holds one asyncio.Lock for each session's whole context, so every other operation waits for the chunk transaction.

Verifier's independent sandboxed run. Native one-line parse took 460/1706/6625 ms at N=4000/8000/16000, against 49/103/216 ms for the same references on N lines. End to end, reindex took 593/1930/7044 ms, and bob's concurrent write waited 295/1645/6685 ms. The N-line control took 592 ms, with bob waiting 284 ms. File SQLite at N=16000: reindex 7090 ms, bob's write waited 6920 ms.

conditions.description: The attacker needs write rights to any one .md path on the mount, for example its own file.
The trusted operator or host runs storage.reindex() on the mount. This is routine maintenance, but it is a storage-direct verb that agents cannot call.

The mount is SQLite-backed (file DatabaseStorage or InMemoryStorage), and other principals write to it while reindex runs. On server engines the chunk transaction holds only row locks, so the cross-writer effect there was not measured. The quadratic CPU, and the delay to the operator's reindex, apply on every engine.

execution.attacker_perspective: A named agent principal (alice) writes one markdown file to a shared mount. Later the operator runs storage.reindex(). Another principal (bob) writes his own unrelated file while the reindex runs.
payloads: fs.write(path='/doc.md', content='[a](b.md) ' * 16000, authority=alice)  # 160 KB, one line
control: fs.write(path='/doc.md', content='[a](b.md)\n' * 16000, authority=alice)  # same bytes and refs, 16000 lines
native: vfs.native.markdown_refs([('[a](b.md) ' * N).encode()]) versus markdown_refs([('[a](b.md)\n' * N).encode()])
instructions: Run agents/v03-p3/scratch/verify.py under tools/sandbox-run.py (no network, empty env, CPU 60 s, wall 120 s, RSS 2 GiB) with ./.venv/bin/python -I.
Time native.markdown_refs at N=4000, 8000 and 16000 for the one-line body and for the N-line body.

For each N, on a fresh InMemoryStorage behind AsyncVirtualFileSystem: alice writes /doc.md, the operator awaits storage.reindex(), and 250 ms in, bob writes /bob.txt. Record the reindex time and bob's write latency. Repeat N=16000 with the N-line control, and on a file-backed SQLite DatabaseStorage.
execution.observed_result: Native one-line: 459.6 / 1705.8 / 6624.5 ms (x3.71, x3.88 per doubling). N-line control: 49.3 / 103.3 / 215.8 ms (linear). In both cases every reference got a 256-char context. InMemoryStorage one-line: reindex 592.6 / 1930.3 / 7044.2 ms, and bob's write waited 295.0 / 1645.5 / 6684.9 ms (it succeeded). N-line control at N=16000: reindex 591.8 ms, bob waited 284.1 ms. File-backed SQLite one-line at N=16000: reindex 7089.9 ms, and bob's write on another pooled connection waited 6920.4 ms, longer than one 5 s busy_timeout, before it succeeded.

remediation.strategy: Make each reference's context cost O(MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS). Compute the newline offsets once per body with memchr and find each reference's line by binary search. References arrive in document order, so cache the folded context per line start and fold each line only once. Make fold_line stop as soon as it has emitted MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS chars. As defence in depth, consider a per-body reference cap or work budget. Also consider running the offloaded CPU before the writer transaction opens, since the chunk flip is already version-guarded. For a regression test, count bytes scanned or fold invocations for one line with N and with 2N references and assert linear growth. Do not assert on wall time.

likelihood.reason: Writing one markdown file is ordinary agent capability, and reindex is routine operator maintenance. The attacker cannot start reindex itself, but every reindex after each rewrite of the file pays the cost again.

impact.reason: On SQLite-backed mounts, every other principal's write blocks for a time that grows quadratically with one file's line length: about 6.7-6.9 s at 160 KB, measured. On InMemoryStorage, all other sessions wait as well. Larger lines extrapolate past busy_timeout times the retry attempts, after which a blocked writer would fail with a conflict. That is inferred from source, not run. The event loop is not stalled, and the stall ends when the pass commits.

confidence.reason: The cited source lines were verified. The native split isolates line_context: the same references and the same inline parse grow linearly when spread over lines and quadratically on one line. The verifier independently reproduced the end-to-end blocking of a concurrent writer on InMemoryStorage and on file SQLite.

title: Grep lines mode copies a separate context window for every hit line, so output grows as hit lines × body size
description: In grep's lines output mode, before_context and after_context are accepted up to 2^31-1. The Rust matcher builds one context span for each hit line and never merges spans that overlap. python.rs then copies each span into its own PyBytes, and grep.py wraps each one in a Match. Nothing limits the size of the output. If the pattern matches every line, or if invert_match is used with a pattern that matches nothing, each of L lines carries about the whole body as its context. The output is then about L × body bytes, which is quadratic in the body. Any caller who can read one multi-line entry can trigger this with a single grep call. allow_scan is not needed, because invert_match takes the scan tier on its own. The memory is allocated in the host process, which many agents share. Local run on InMemoryStorage: a 40,000-byte body of 4,000 lines returned 159,996,000 characters of match content, and peak RSS rose to about 634 MB. Each doubling of L multiplied the output by 4.
root_cause: extend_context (crates/vfs-core/src/verify.rs:242) builds a full span for each hit line on its own. Matcher::hit_lines (verify.rs:118) pushes one span per hit and only stops at max_count, which defaults to None. Overlapping windows are never merged. python.rs:154 copies each span into a new PyBytes, and grep.py:358 wraps each in a Match. Nothing bounds the output: CONTENT_BYTE_BUDGET (grep.py:126) only limits input bodies held at once, the parameter gate allows context up to INT_CEILING, and the wall-time deadline is checked only before each body starts (verify.rs:197), never inside one.
intended_behavior: Grep's lines-mode output should stay bounded by about the size of the matched body, whatever the context arguments are. That is how the ripgrep baseline behaves: it merges overlapping or adjacent context windows and emits each line at most once. The repo's own early spec expected the same ('merged context windows render correctly', context/specifications/archive/001-unify-vfs-result-and-optimize-queries/spec.md:169). Failing that, a declared output budget should truncate the result with a classified warning, as grep's other budgets do.

trace.description: The caller's before_context and after_context are accepted as ints from 0 to INT_CEILING (2^31-1). Lines 278-286 do the same for after_context. max_count (line 288) is optional and defaults to None.
Passes before_context, after_context and cap=max_count (None by default) to VerifyOffload.hit_lines for each content batch. No output budget is applied.
Pushes one extend_context span for every hit line. It stops only at cap, so with no cap every line gets its own span.

Walks back up to `before` lines and forward up to `after` lines from each hit, clamped only to the body. With huge context each span is the whole body. Spans are not merged with the previous hit's span.
Copies the bytes of every span into a new PyBytes while holding the GIL. Total allocation is the sum of all span lengths, about hits × body bytes.
Wraps each span's content in a pydantic Match on the event loop. The quadratic payload is kept in Observation.matches and returned to the caller.

evidence.description: hits.push(extend_context(...)) runs once per hit line, and the cap is the only stop condition.
extend_context computes a span per hit on its own. There is no merge with earlier spans.

title: Chained grep over observations runs regex verification on the event loop with no wall, candidate or byte budget, amplified by duplicate rows
description: grep(observations=...) goes to _grep_rows_in_hand. That function reads the content of every listed row that has no content attached, in one self.read call. It then calls match_texts with budget=None, synchronously on the event-loop thread. The storage-tier grep does the same verification work under several controls: a 25,000-candidate budget, 32 MiB content chunks, a 10 s wall deadline, and an offload to an executor (its own comment says 'Verify leaves the loop'). The chained path applies none of these. Rows are not deduplicated, so a caller can list one stored file it may read N times; the file is fetched once and verified N times. Loop occupancy therefore grows linearly with N x body bytes x the per-byte cost of the pattern, and the pattern length has no cap. Every other coroutine on that loop is stalled until the native call returns. That includes every thread sharing one sync VirtualFileSystem facade, which serves all its callers from one loop thread. This was reproduced locally: one stored file of about 0.98 MB, the pattern (\w|\s){60}Q, and 10, 20 and 40 duplicate Observations blocked the loop for 0.65 s, 1.22 s and 2.70 s. The storage-tier scan of the same file and pattern never blocked the loop for more than 13 ms.
root_cause: _grep_rows_in_hand (src/vfs/base.py:1919) calls pattern_matching.grep.match_texts, which passes budget=None to ContentMatcher.count_lines/hit_lines (src/vfs/pattern_matching/grep.py:252,259). It makes this call inline on the coroutine's thread. It does not use the storage tier's VerifyOffload, byte_chunked(CONTENT_BYTE_BUDGET), CANDIDATE_BUDGET or WALL_TIME_BUDGET controls. The observations list has no length cap and is not deduplicated, and the pattern has no length cap.
intended_behavior: Content verification should carry the same bounds whether its rows come from storage or from observations=. That means running off the event loop on the backend's executor, under a wall-time deadline that truncates with a warning, with bodies processed in byte-budgeted batches, and with each distinct body verified at most once per call. The storage tier already declares and enforces exactly this contract.

Every candidate row without content is read in a single self.read(observations=absent) call, with no candidate or byte budget. A row that already carries content needs no read at all.
match_texts runs over every texted row, duplicates included, synchronously on the event-loop thread.

Every body is matched to completion across rayon threads. The binding releases the GIL (python.rs py.detach), but the calling loop thread waits for the whole batch.

_observation_rows only type-checks the batch. It applies no length cap and no deduplication.
VirtualFileSystem owns one asyncio loop on one daemon thread (lines 647-648). Every thread that calls one facade shares that loop, so a stall on it is shared within the library itself.

Local run: one 975,000-byte stored file, pattern (\w|\s){60}Q, files mode. The loop was blocked 0.654 s at 10 duplicate rows, 1.222 s at 20 and 2.703 s at 40. The storage scan tier on the same file had a 0.013 s maximum loop gap (line 23).
The script that produced growth-output.txt. It runs a 1 ms asyncio ticker beside fs.grep(observations=[Observation(path=/data/big.txt)] * N) and records the largest loop gap.

Pattern calibration. Literal-prefiltered patterns finished in milliseconds. (\w|\s){60}Q cost about 0.43 s per MB: it blocked the loop on the chained path (gap 0.418-0.465 s) but not on the storage tier (gap 0.012 s).

The host serves several agents or principals from one AsyncVirtualFileSystem event loop, or from one sync VirtualFileSystem facade (one loop thread by construction), and passes agent-supplied observations and patterns through without a size limit.

Start a coroutine that sleeps 1 ms in a loop and records the largest gap between wakeups.

Second, run the matcher off the loop through VerifyOffload on an executor, or through asyncio.to_thread when no backend executor is available. Third, pass a wall-time deadline derived from WALL_TIME_BUDGET and truncate with a warning when it trips. Fourth, process bodies in byte_chunked(CONTENT_BYTE_BUDGET) batches, checking the deadline between batches. A host-side cap on observations length and pattern length is additional defense in depth.

hits = [hits_unique[unique[(str(row.path), text)]] for row, text in texted]

Every coroutine and every sync-facade caller sharing the loop stalls for a time proportional to N x body size x pattern cost, with no deadline; about 2.7 s was observed at N=40 on 1 MB, and it grows linearly. Nothing persists and no data is exposed, and the loop recovers when the call returns. The synchronous native call cannot be cancelled.

title: Glob patterns compile to backtracking Python regex with no cap on wildcards, so one glob call can stall the shared event loop
description: A caller who can run glob, or grep/glean with glob channels, sends a short pattern with k wildcard pairs such as '*?' repeated k times, plus a '[...]' class. vfs turns each '*' into a backtracking [^/]* and compiles it with CPython re. Matching against one stored name of length n then costs roughly O(n^k). The match runs synchronously on the asyncio event loop for every candidate row, and it runs before the visibility check (view.shows). So rows the caller cannot see still cost time. The '[' class makes the SQL LIKE prefilter fall back to an empty literal prefix plus '%', so every live row in the mount is a candidate. The path-segment cap of 255 bytes bounds n for each name. Nothing bounds k or the pattern length. Local reproduction on a fresh InMemoryStorage with the default caller: '*?*?*?*?[Q]' against one 250-character name blocked the loop for 0.85 s, and '*?*?*?*?*?*?[Q]' against one 64-character name blocked it for 0.54 s. A concurrent unrelated glob had to wait the whole time. Cost also grows linearly with the number of candidate rows: 10 rows with 128-character names took 0.61 s, against 0.07 s for one.
root_cause: _translate and _translate_component (src/vfs/pattern_matching/glob.py) emit [^/]* for each '*' and (?:.+/)? for each non-final '**', with no limit on how many wildcards or how long the pattern is. compile_glob compiles the result with Python re, which backtracks, instead of the linear-time Rust regex engine that vfs-core already uses for grep. glob_rows runs passes_row_filters, and so the regex, inline on the event loop for every SQL candidate, before view.shows, with no deadline. _glob_like returns None for any '[' class, so the prefilter matches every row.
intended_behavior: Glob matching should take time linear in the subject length, as the Rust regex engine used by grep does. Otherwise it should be bounded by a wildcard or pattern-length cap and a deadline, so one caller's glob cannot block other agents on the same loop.

trace.description: Public verb that accepts a caller pattern string. Neither it nor the params gate caps pattern length or wildcard count.
_glob_like returns None for a '[' class, so the prefilter becomes escape_like(literal_prefix) + '%'. With an empty literal prefix, every live row in the mount is a SQL candidate.
passes_row_filters runs the compiled glob regex on each candidate row, synchronously on the loop, before view.shows (line 370) applies visibility.
Each '*' becomes the backtracking [^/]*. compile_glob (line 208) compiles it with Python re.compile, which gives O(n^k) failing matches.

evidence.description: compile_glob returns re.compile(_translate(_canonical(pattern), recursive=True)), which uses the backtracking CPython engine.
A non-final '**' component becomes (?:.+/)?, which also backtracks across segments of path-subject patterns.
_glob_like returns None whenever '[' appears in the pattern, which disables the selective LIKE prefilter.
The strongest pattern-side control: MAX_PATTERN_ARMS = 64 caps brace expansion only. It does not cap wildcard count or pattern length.
MAX_SEGMENT_LENGTH = 255 bytes caps n for each name-subject match, but it does not cap the polynomial degree k. At n=250, k=4 already costs about 0.85 s for each row.

Verifier's sandboxed reproduction. k=4 at n=64/128/250 took 0.014/0.070/0.854 s, k=6 at n=48/64 took 0.12/0.54 s, and 10 rows at k=4, n=128 took 0.61 s. The largest event-loop gap and a concurrent victim glob's latency each matched the attacking glob's duration. The benign control '*.txt' took 0.016 s.

conditions.description: The caller can invoke glob, or grep/glean with glob channels, on a mount. The reproduction used the default router caller on a fresh InMemoryStorage. Visibility does not gate the cost, because the regex runs before view.shows.

The mount holds rows whose names or path segments are tens of characters or longer (up to 255 bytes for each segment). Cost scales with the number of live rows in the mount, because the '[' class disables the prefilter.
The host serves several agents or callers from one process and asyncio event loop, so a stall on that loop delays every other caller.

execution.attacker_perspective: An agent with glob access to an AsyncVirtualFileSystem whose event loop is shared with other agents.
instructions: Inside the sandbox, build AsyncVirtualFileSystem(storage=InMemoryStorage()) and write one file whose leaf name is n characters long (n <= 255), plus an unrelated small file.
Start a 1 ms asyncio ticker and a concurrent victim task that globs '/small.txt'.
Await fs.glob(payload) and record the glob duration, the largest gap between ticker wakeups, and the victim's glob latency. Compare with a benign '*.txt' glob.
execution.observed_result: Python 3.13.11. For k=4: 0.014 s at n=64, 0.070 s at n=128 and 0.854 s at n=250. For k=6: 0.12 s at n=48 and 0.54 s at n=64. With k=4, n=128, 10 rows took 0.61 s. Each call returned zero rows and no errors. The largest event-loop gap was within a few ms of each glob's duration (for example 0.848 s at k=4, n=250). The concurrent victim glob took the same 0.85 s. The benign '*.txt' glob over the same 10 rows took 0.016 s. A 256-byte segment was refused (the segment cap), which bounds n but not k.

remediation.strategy: Compile glob regexes with the linear-time Rust regex engine already in vfs-core, or with a non-backtracking glob matcher, for compile_glob, compile_filter and _component_matches. Until then, refuse patterns above a declared wildcard count and pattern length in glob_defect/expand_pattern. Also consider applying view.shows before the regex, or running the per-row matching under the same deadline grep uses. Add a regression test that runs a fixed adversarial pattern and asserts on an operation count (matcher calls or steps), not on time.

impact.reason: Each call blocks the shared event loop for every co-hosted agent, for up to about a second for each long-named row at k=4 and more for larger k or more rows. The stall is temporary and recovers when the call ends. Repeated calls can sustain it. There is no persistence, and no effect on confidentiality or integrity.

title: Repeated docx footnote or comment references copy the full note text inline before the character budget applies
description: The docx renderer writes a note's text inline at each footnoteReference or commentReference. _Writer._inline makes a fresh formatted copy of the full note text for every reference, keeps every copy in a list, joins them into one string, and only then hands that string to Builder.paragraph. Builder.paragraph runs sanitize() and splitlines() over the whole string before _append checks any budget. So a paragraph that repeats one reference N times to a note of L characters builds about N x L characters in memory, plus further copies, before RenderLimits.chars or the ratio guard can act. This grows with the product of two values the writer chooses, not with the decompressed input. Repeated references and repeated note text compress almost to nothing. In the sandbox, a 2,783-byte docx (one 10,000-character footnote, 10,000 references) reached a traced peak of 191.5 MiB inside DocxRenderer.render. The growth was linear: 1.9 MiB at 100 references, 19.2 MiB at 1,000 and 191.5 MiB at 10,000. A 13,970-byte docx built the same way (a 100,000-character note, 100,000 references) implies 10^10 inline characters, about 10 GB. That case was built and measured only, not rendered. Rendering runs in DatabaseStorage.reindex on the offload pool of the host process that all agents share. Because the copies build up one note at a time rather than in one huge allocation, the likely end is that the OS kills the process or the host swaps heavily, not a MemoryError that the registry would catch. A killed render never lands its stamp, so the row stays render_status='pending' and every later reindex renders it again.
root_cause: _Writer._inline (src/vfs/rendering/docx.py:131-149) appends _note(...) for every footnoteReference and commentReference with no limit on how many copies or how many characters it collects. Each _note call formats a new string holding the full note text (docx.py:152-154). The result is ''.join(parts), built in full before Builder sees it. Builder enforces RenderLimits.chars and the ratio guard only per line in _append (markdown.py:275-289), after paragraph() has already run sanitize(text).splitlines() over the whole string (markdown.py:180). The ratio guard compares output characters with the compressed input size, and only after the text exists.
intended_behavior: RenderLimits.chars (2 MiB by default) and the ratio guard should bound what a renderer builds, not only what it emits. The docx module docstring says 'the character budget bounds a document'. Inline note assembly should stop once the paragraph can no longer fit in the Builder's remaining budget, or write each note's text once and mark later references by id, so that memory stays within a small multiple of the budget whatever the reference count.

The operator's reindex selects every dirty bytes row, with no authority filter, and renders it through render_rows on the shared offload pool (call_offloaded at line 1288).
text, pictures = self._inline(paragraph._p): the whole paragraph string is built before the Builder is called.
parts.append(_note('footnote', ...)) runs for every footnoteReference (and line 146 for commentReference). Each call is a fresh copy of the full note text, and line 149 joins them all with no budget.

Builder.paragraph runs sanitize(text).splitlines() over the whole joined string before any per-line budget check.
The character budget and, at line 287, the ratio guard are checked only per appended line, after the text has been built.
The registry catches only Exception. An OS kill of the process or heavy swapping is not caught, so the row stays pending.

Sandbox run with a 10,000-character footnote. Traced peak inside DocxRenderer.render: 0.2 MiB at 0 references, 1.9 MiB at 100, 19.2 MiB at 1,000 and 191.5 MiB at 10,000. Input size stayed between 1,505 and 2,783 bytes.
Size-only build, not rendered: a 13,970-byte docx (100,000-character note, 100,000 references) implies 10^10 inline characters, and a 15,713-byte docx (1,000,000-character note) implies 10^11.
The reproduction script. It builds a minimal docx with dummy text and measures tracemalloc peak during DocxRenderer().render with the default RenderLimits.

title: A docx table cell's gridSpan value expands into an unbounded cell list before any render limit applies
description: _Writer.table builds rows = [[cell.text for cell in row.cells] for row in table.rows] and only then hands the rows to Builder.table. In the installed python-docx 1.2.0, _Row.cells yields the same _Cell once for each grid column the cell spans (iter_tc_cells: for _ in range(tc.grid_span): yield cell). grid_span is read straight from the w:tcPr/w:gridSpan/@val integer and is never compared with the table's real grid width. The renderer then calls cell.text once for each yielded entry, and each call builds a new string. So one attribute in a document of about 36 KB decides how many tuple entries, cell.text calls and list strings get created. All of this work finishes before Builder sees the first row. The character budget, the ratio guard, the unit cap and the cooperative clock (RenderLimits.seconds, checked only at block boundaries and between table rows) therefore do not bound it. The bytes come from any principal allowed to write(data=...) to a DatabaseStorage mount; the write stores them as render_status='pending'. The expansion runs later, when the operator calls reindex(). It runs on the backend's in-process ThreadPoolExecutor, the pool that grep's verify stage also uses, and a running worker cannot be interrupted. Local run: input size held constant at about 36.7 KB (36,703 to 36,705 bytes), gridSpan raised from 1e3 to 1e6. cell.text calls grew exactly linearly (1,000 to 1,000,000). Peak RSS rose from 113.6 MiB to 473.0 MiB. Wall time was about 22 s against RenderLimits(seconds=1.0); this is informational only. Spans of 1e5 and above also return status 'empty' with no text, because the header line alone overflows the character budget. Correction to the hunter's wording: a render that completes lands a terminal state and is not retried. A row stays pending, and is retried on every reindex, only when the span is large enough that the render never finishes or the process dies. The schema allows values up to 2^31-1. That size was not executed: by extrapolation it is more than 16 GiB of tuple pointers alone, plus hours of CPU.
root_cause: DocxRenderer's table path builds the span-expanded row.cells tuple and one cell.text string per grid position, with no cap and no clamp to the table's declared grid width. RenderLimits are enforced only inside Builder, on text it emits. The materialization runs as one uninterruptible step on the offload thread, before any of those checks.
intended_behavior: A render's memory and CPU should stay bounded by RenderLimits and roughly proportional to the input bytes. Per the seam's own docstring, a malformed or hostile docx should end as a classified 'truncated' or 'failed' state within the time budget, not do work set by an attribute value.

title: An xlsx sheet's declared dimension and far-off row index drive padded cell iteration that the render clock never checks
description: XlsxRenderer opens workbooks with read_only=True. In openpyxl 3.1.5, ReadOnlyWorksheet takes max_column and max_row from the sheet's <dimension ref>. Then _cells_by_row yields a padding row (one shared tuple of max_column EMPTY_CELLs) for every missing row between two populated rows. vfs's _cells() walks every yielded cell and checks no clock, cell budget or row budget. The deadline is consulted only after _cells returns, in Builder.table and Builder.unit. So a file of about 4.7 KB, with one cell at A1, one cell at A<R> and a dimension of A1:ZZZ<R>, makes one render iterate 18,278 x R cells. Columns are capped at ZZZ (18,278) by openpyxl; the row index is a plain int with no cap. Measured in the sandbox, with RenderLimits(seconds=0.5): 365,560,000 cells took 3.24 s, and 50,000,000 padded rows took 3.34 s, both about 6.5x over the limit. Cost is linear at about 9 ns per cell, so A1:ZZZ1048576 projects to roughly 170 s, and a row index of 10^8 projects to hours, all against the 60 s RENDER_SECONDS default. This happens during the operator's reindex, on an offload worker that cannot be interrupted. The single-runner reindex lease keeps its heartbeat, so the lease stays held and every other subject's pending render, chunk and posting work waits behind it. The row is landed only after its cut finishes, so a run that is abandoned leaves the row pending, and the next reindex starts the same work again. Correction to the hunter: an empty sheetData, or a lone A1 with a huge dimension, does NOT pad. openpyxl's tail-padding guard is 'max_row < idx' (_read_only.py:100), so the trailing rows are never yielded; this was measured as 26 cells for dimension A1:Z100000 with only A1. The attack needs a second populated row at the far end, which uses the in-between gap padding (_read_only.py:92).
root_cause: _cells() (src/vfs/rendering/xlsx.py:161-172) walks sheet.iter_rows() over openpyxl's dimension-padded read-only grid. It takes no Builder, deadline or cell or row budget. The cooperative clock in Builder covers only the Builder calls that come after _cells has collected the whole sheet. So the iteration work grows with the declared extent (columns x row gap), not with the input bytes, and no RenderLimits field bounds it.
intended_behavior: RenderLimits.seconds (RENDER_SECONDS, 'Wall seconds one render may spend before the text so far is kept as partial') should bound each render. Once the clock runs out, an xlsx render should stop within a small constant amount of work and return partial. The work should be proportional to the cells actually stored, not to the dimension or row numbers the file declares.

title: xlsx region layout does quadratic work on writer-shaped cell layouts before any render budget applies
description: A subject that can write a bytes entry stores a small .xlsx file. The operator's reindex later renders it with the bundled XlsxRenderer, on the shared offload pool inside the host process. regions() joins cells that touch by side or by corner. So an L-shape (R cells down column A, then C cells across the last row) or a diagonal of n cells becomes one region whose bounding box is R x C, or n x n. _table() then builds the whole box as Python lists, header plus body, (bottom-top+1) x (right-left+1) entries, before Builder.table() emits its first row. The character budget, the output/input ratio guard and the clock are only checked inside Builder, so they act after that allocation has already happened. Observed locally: a 56,977-byte workbook made 32,012,001 table entries and a 270.9 MB traced peak during DatabaseStorage.reindex() on SQLite, and the rendering still landed as 'rendered'. Doubling both sides quadrupled the peak (68.7 MB, then 270.9 MB), while the file grew less than 2x. Separately, _merged() compares each region box with every box already kept, so k isolated cells cost k(k-1)/2 overlap checks: 400 cells made 79,800 calls and 6,400 cells made 20,476,800. That work also runs before any budget and never reads the clock. The module docstring says the region pass is linear. Neither of these two steps is linear.
root_cause: In src/vfs/rendering/xlsx.py, _table() builds every grid position of a region's bounding box as a list of lists, and _merged() does pairwise overlap checks over all region boxes. Both run in full before control reaches Builder, and Builder is the only place RenderLimits (chars, ratio, seconds) are enforced. Box area and region count depend on how the writer lays out cells, not on the input size or on the output budget.
intended_behavior: Per the xlsx module docstring and RenderLimits: one render holds memory linear in a sheet's non-empty cell count, the region pass is linear, and the character budget and wall clock bound the work spent on any one rendering, so a small input cannot make the renderer allocate or compute far beyond what it can emit.

title: OOXML parts are fully decompressed into host memory before any render limit applies, so a small docx can cost hundreds of times its size in RSS during reindex
description: The docx and pptx renderers pass the stored bytes straight to docx.Document and pptx.Presentation. vfs checks no zip entry sizes, compression ratios or member counts first. When python-docx 1.2.0 opens a package, it walks every internal relationship and calls ZipFile.read on each target part. python-pptx 1.0.2 goes further and reads every zip member, referenced or not, into a dict. Every RenderLimits check runs inside Builder, on output characters, after this expansion has already happened. The RENDER_RATIO comment calls the ratio the decompression-bomb guard, but a part that decompresses large and yields no text never reaches it. Rendering runs on the DatabaseStorage offload ThreadPoolExecutor, which is inside the host process all agents share. I reproduced this locally. One docx stored at 442,096 bytes, holding one relationship-referenced 400 MiB part of zeros, raised peak RSS by 805 MiB in a direct registry render and by 807 MiB in a real write-then-reindex on SQLite. That is about 1,900 times the stored size. The render still returned status ok with text 'hello quokka', and no limit fired. Because deflate tops out near 1000:1 and the library holds the blob, a stored body of a few MiB can be enough to exhaust the host's memory.
root_cause: DocxRenderer.render (docx.py:50) and PptxRenderer.render (pptx.py:38) open caller-supplied zip containers with libraries that eagerly decompress part blobs (docx/opc/pkgreader.py:79 via phys_pkg.py:83 ZipFile.read; pptx/opc/serialized.py:195 reads every member). vfs does no central-directory inspection before that call. Every RenderLimits check (chars, ratio, units, seconds) lives in Builder, which measures emitted text after expansion, so input-side decompression has no bound at all.
intended_behavior: A render's memory should be bounded by declared limits relative to the stored input, as the seam's 'decompression-bomb guard' comment says. An OOXML body whose declared total uncompressed size, single-entry size, member count or compression ratio exceeds a RenderLimits cap should be refused as a classified 'failed' or 'corrupt' state before the parsing library decompresses anything.

remediation.strategy: Before calling any OOXML library, open the body with zipfile.ZipFile and inspect infolist(). Refuse with a classified failed/corrupt Rendering when any of these exceeds a declared RenderLimits field: the member count, any entry's file_size, the sum of file_size, or the file_size/compress_size ratio. import zipfile
from io import BytesIO

RENDER_PACKAGE_BYTES: Final = 256 * 1024 * 1024
RENDER_PACKAGE_MEMBERS: Final = 10_000
RENDER_MEMBER_RATIO: Final = 200


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RenderLimits:
    """The caps one render runs inside; a host may lower them, never raise the ratio."""

    chars: int = RENDER_CHARS
    ratio: int = RENDER_RATIO
    embedded_depth: int = RENDER_EMBEDDED_DEPTH
    embedded_count: int = RENDER_EMBEDDED_COUNT
    pages: int = RENDER_PAGES
    seconds: float = RENDER_SECONDS
    package_bytes: int = RENDER_PACKAGE_BYTES
    package_members: int = RENDER_PACKAGE_MEMBERS
    member_ratio: int = RENDER_MEMBER_RATIO
    # __post_init__ also checks the three new fields are positive


def package_refusal(data: bytes, limits: RenderLimits) -> str | None:
    """Why a zip container is refused before any library decompresses it, or None."""
    try:
        infos = zipfile.ZipFile(BytesIO(data)).infolist()
    except (zipfile.BadZipFile, ValueError) as exc:
        return f"not a zip container: {exc}"
    if len(infos) > limits.package_members:
        return f"{len(infos)} members exceed {limits.package_members}"
    total = sum(i.file_size for i in infos)
    if total > limits.package_bytes:
        return f"{total} uncompressed bytes exceed {limits.package_bytes}"
    for i in infos:
        if i.file_size > RENDER_RATIO_FLOOR and i.file_size > limits.member_ratio * max(1, i.compress_size):
            return f"{i.filename} expands {i.file_size}/{i.compress_size}"
    return None

title: A write, move or copy that read the everyone posture before a tightening posture commit can stamp the old, more open everyone_level after the relabel has cleared its mark
description: entries.everyone_level is a derived copy of the deepest everyone ('*') posture on a row's path. Once no relabel mark stands over a path, Rights.admits trusts the stored label outright. Posture writes take the admin lock with bump_revision, and every Relabeller chunk takes it with hold_revision. The mint paths take neither. write and mkdir call labels_for at writes.py:379, and move and copy call posture_beneath at topology.py:197. Both read the grants rows with plain SELECTs and never re-check the relabels table. Here is the interleaving. A write W pins its snapshot at its first statement, because op_isolation is REPEATABLE READ on Postgres and MariaDB. A posture commit P then tightens /eng/secret.md to none. The path need not hold a row, per _grant_refusal at rights.py:1318. P's Relabeller runs and clears the mark while W is still open. It cannot see W's uncommitted insert. When the posture sits at the created path, it rewrites 0 rows. W then commits with the old label. After that, any named principal with no grant can read the row, and anonymous grep and glob list it. Nothing in src corrects the label: rebuild_labels has no caller there. I re-ran the hunter's consequence emulation on SQLite in the sandbox: the mint is handed the labels that the real labels_for and posture_beneath computed before the posture commit. Results with no pending marks: write, move and copy stamp everyone_level=2 under posture none. bob (no grants) reads 'TOPSECRET payroll'. Anonymous and bob grep and glob list /eng/secret.md. Anonymous direct read stays refused (unauthenticated). bob's overwrite stays refused, because read is below the write rung. The control with fresh labels gives label 0 and not_found. rebuild_labels repairs the label. The real interleaving cannot happen on SQLite, because writers hold BEGIN IMMEDIATE. So the decisive concurrent behaviour on a real engine has not been observed. The spec that introduced the label (context/specifications/archive/150-rights-at-scale/spec.md) analyses rival admin writes, but not a concurrent mint against a relabel.
claimed_root_cause: labels_for (labels.py:124, reading posture_rows at labels.py:110-121) and posture_beneath (labels.py:139) read the everyone posture rows without the admin revision lock (no hold_revision, nothing that conflicts with bump_revision) and without consulting inflight relabel marks. The Relabeller (labels.py:244-266) rewrites only rows visible to its own statements, then deletes the mark. A mint whose posture read predates a posture commit, and which commits after that posture's relabel has passed its path, therefore stamps a stale label that no mark covers. readers then trust it (grants.py:491).

trace.description: The write verb, called by a named principal holding write rights (alice), runs its plan through _execute_write (backend.py:1666-1673) with op_execution_options(writer=True). On Postgres and MariaDB that stamps isolation_level REPEATABLE READ (dialects.py:593-594), so the snapshot is pinned at the first statement.
labels_for is called for the creates after staging. Nothing in writes.py takes hold_revision or bump_revision, issues a locking read, or reads the relabels table.
A plain SELECT of the '*' grants rows over the ancestor prefixes. Under W's pinned snapshot it returns the posture as it stood before a concurrent posture commit.

Move and copy compute posture_beneath with the same unlocked read, after the serialize() lock-table point (topology.py:143), which is not the revision lock. They stamp the result at topology.py:315 (moved root), 373 (descendants) and 453 (copied rows), under topology_isolation READ COMMITTED.

The posture write upserts the '*' row and plants the relabel mark in one transaction, after bump_revision (backend.py:1594). _grant_refusal (rights.py:1318) lets the path hold no row, so a posture can be set at a path a concurrent write is creating.

Each chunk takes hold_revision and rewrites the rows its statements see. It cannot see W's uncommitted rows; for a posture at a not-yet-existing path it rewrites 0 rows (observed: relabel rows=0). The last chunk deletes the mark and bumps the revision (labels.py:265-266).

With no hole standing (the mark is gone), a row whose stored everyone_level reaches the needed rung is admitted. Named callers' reads, and grep and glob for anonymous and named callers alike, then admit the stale-labelled row.

evidence.description: The module docstring says the label is derived, stamped at every mint from the posture rows, and covered by the mark only while the relabel is in flight. Nothing ties the mint's read to the lock that orders posture commits.

hold_revision is the admin lock that relabel chunks take, so they serialize behind rival admin writes. The mint paths take neither it nor bump_revision (no revision import in writes.py or topology.py).

Postgres declares op_isolation REPEATABLE READ, and MariaDB does the same at line 500. op_execution_options (line 582) applies it to writer connections, so the write's posture read comes from its first statement's snapshot.

The strongest visible control. unauthenticated_at judges anonymous path-addressed calls from the posture rows, not the label, so an anonymous direct read stays refused (observed). Named callers and the anonymous list and search verbs still trust the label.
On SQLite, writers open BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so a posture commit cannot land inside a write's window. That is why the real interleaving cannot be observed locally.
The in-flight rule covers stale labels only while the mark stands. The spec's race analysis (line 242) covers rival admin writes, not a mint that is concurrent with a relabel.

My sandboxed SQLite re-run of the hunter's consequence emulation. Fresh-label control: label 0, bob not_found. Mint given the pre-commit posture read: everyone_level=2 under posture none with no marks. bob reads TOPSECRET content, and anonymous grep and glob list the path. Anonymous direct read and bob's overwrite stay refused. rebuild_labels resets the label to 0. The relabel rewrote 0 rows for the posture at the created path.

blockers: The decisive concurrent interleaving cannot happen on SQLite. Writers hold BEGIN IMMEDIATE from the plan's first read (engine.py:649-655), and a deferred SQLite reader could not upgrade a stale snapshot to a write anyway. Real engines (Postgres, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle) and Docker are prohibited in this sandbox. Only the consequence was observed, by handing the mint its pre-commit posture read.

Postgres REPEATABLE READ: the source predicts that a posture at the created path, or at a directory the same batch creates, leaves W's existing parent outside the relabelled region. Then no 40001 conflict arises and W commits the stale label. Where the posture covers an existing parent, the relabel rewrites that parent, so W's guarded parent bump (_bump_parents, writes.py:1026) should fail with a serialization error and redrive. Neither outcome has been observed on a live engine.

MariaDB: whether innodb_snapshot_isolation (ON by default from 11.6, error 1020) turns the parent bump into a restart, and whether a Relabeller range UPDATE (a current read) blocks on a concurrently moved row's uncommitted index entry and then relabels it, are both unobserved.

SQL Server (no op_isolation): under locking READ COMMITTED, the relabel UPDATE may block on W's uncommitted key and then relabel it, which narrows the window to the gap between labels_for and the insert. Under READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT it would skip the row. Which mode a deployment runs is a database setting outside source.

Oracle: the statement-level consistent read in the relabel UPDATE is expected to skip uncommitted inserted or moved rows, leaving the window open from labels_for or posture_beneath to commit. Unobserved.

title: copy, sweep, delete and move check rights over a subtree once, then act on rows read later, including rows a concurrent writer just added
description: The topology and trash verbs check the caller's rights over the source subtree once, inside the gate (WriteGate.subtrees). That check reads the rows beneath the root as they exist at that moment. The later statements read the subtree again, live, and act on whatever they find. Copy and move fetch the subtree with _fetch_subtree and _descendant_rewrites. Delete marks every live descendant with one LIKE update. The sweep purge loops its select-then-delete until the scope reads empty. Nothing checks the rows found by these later reads. The serialization point only makes serialized verbs wait for each other. Ordinary writes never read the lock row. On the server engines the topology transaction runs at READ COMMITTED, so every statement sees rows committed after the gate. Example: alice holds rights over /team/alice only through the owner floor, and bob holds add there. If bob's file commits inside the window, alice's copy duplicates it into /mine/c, owned by alice with the destination label, and alice can then read a file the read verb hides from her. Alice's sweep in the same window permanently destroys bob's file. Run one after the other, both calls are permission_denied. Some guards narrow the window, though they do not close it. In move and delete, a direct child that commits after the snapshot bumps the root's version, so the root claim misses and the verb redrives, which re-runs the gate. That guard does not cover the window between the gate and the snapshot. It also misses a deeper descendant, whose write bumps only its own parent. Copy and the sweep purge arm have no root guard at all. In the sweep, the rival does not even need precise timing: the purge's delete of the root waits on the rival's parent-bump row lock, and the re-collect loop then finds the rival's row and deletes it. The repository's own threat model (T57 in context/research/2026-09-05-permissions-framing-threat-model-and-requirements.md) says check and act must happen in one statement or one transaction, with the write's own predicate as the check. Here the check and the act share a transaction, but under READ COMMITTED the act's predicate is not the check. I re-ran this independently. The rival write was injected at the repository's own seams (transfer:post-snapshot and purge:post-collect) on the verb's own session. With it, alice's copy succeeded and she read 'BOB SECRET' from /mine/c/s.txt, and alice's sweep succeeded and bob's file was gone. The sequential controls were permission_denied. This simulates READ COMMITTED visibility; it is not a commit from a second connection. Likely fix: inside the mutation, judge every collected row with resolution.at(rung).admits(path, owner_id, everyone_level), and refuse or redrive on a miss. That covers copy's subtree, move's descendant rewrites, delete's descendant stamp (as a RETURNING set or a pre-stamp select), and each purge collect. Another option is to make child creation take a shared lock that conflicts with the serialization row.
claimed_root_cause: The authorization decision (WriteGate.subtrees, rights.py:730-761, paging through _refused_beneath at rights.py:763-780) runs over a point-in-time read. The scope the mutation acts on is collected again afterwards by path pattern: topology.py:186 (_fetch_subtree, copy and move), topology.py:397 (_descendant_rewrites, move), trash.py:483 (_tombstone_descendants, delete) and trash.py:567 (the _purge collect loop, sweep). Rows found by these later reads are never judged. Ordinary writes do not serialize with these verbs (serialized.py:115-123). The topology connection is pinned to READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and MariaDB (dialects.py:437, 503). MSSQL and Oracle declare no pin, so they run at their engine default of READ COMMITTED (dialects.py:607-609). Each later statement therefore sees rows committed after the gate.

trace.description: A named lower-trust caller's copy or move source is authorized by checks.subtrees(sources, passing) at read or read_write. delete (backend.py:763) and sweep (backend.py:862) make the same subtree call at read_write.
Pages through the rows beneath the root that exist when this statement runs, and checks each with rights.admits. A row committed afterwards is never judged.
A locking read of the single lock row. Its docstring (line 117) says nothing else reads that row, so ordinary writes commit concurrently with copy, move, delete and sweep.

After the gate and the per-pair checks, the source subtree is read again live through subtree_filter. Under READ COMMITTED it includes a rival's newly committed rows. Copy takes no lock or version guard on the source root.
The sweep purge arm repeats collect-then-delete until the scope reads empty, which is meant to catch late children. It hard-deletes them with no rights check and no proof predicate (trash.py:381).

Every collected row, the rival's included, is minted at the destination with owner_id = owner_for(authority) and the destination posture label (line 453). _copy_bodies (topology.py:483-517) then copies its body, so the copier owns a readable duplicate.

evidence.description: _tombstone_descendants marks every live row under the claimed directory. Its docstring says a child a rival landed after the snapshot rides with its parent. The root version guard (trash.py:200-202) catches only a direct child that commits after the snapshot; a deeper descendant, or any child in the gate-to-snapshot window, is tombstoned without being judged.

The sweep purge arm calls _purge with subtree_filter and no proof. The _purge docstring (trash.py:551-554) says writes are not serialized with this verb and the loop exists to catch a rival's new child.
Move rewrites the descendants it collects live after the root claim. A late deeper descendant is relocated to the destination and takes the destination's label without being judged.

PostgreSQL topology_isolation is READ COMMITTED. MariaDB matches at line 503, and topology_execution_options (dialects.py:598-610) leaves MSSQL and Oracle on their READ COMMITTED default. Each statement sees rows committed after the gate.
subtrees skips the read only when the caller's rights cover the subtree whole. The gap opens exactly where rights are partial: an owner floor, or a posture that narrows a region.
_bump_parents: a write bumps only its immediate parent's version. So a root version guard sees only direct-child arrivals, and copy and sweep check no root version at all.

Verifier's independent run on InMemoryStorage. Bob's legitimate write is injected at the repository's own seams on the verb's session. Controls: alice cannot read bob's file, and her sequential copy and sweep are permission_denied. Raced: the copy succeeds and alice reads 'BOB SECRET' from /mine/c/s.txt; the sweep succeeds and bob's file is gone.

blockers: The decisive interleaving needs a real commit from a second connection on a server engine (PostgreSQL, MSSQL, MariaDB or Oracle) during the verb's transaction. This sandbox allows only SQLite and InMemoryStorage. There, topology verbs open BEGIN IMMEDIATE and hold the database write lock, so a second writer cannot commit inside the window.

The local evidence (the hunter's and mine) injects the rival write on the victim verb's own session at the repository's seams. That simulates READ COMMITTED statement visibility. It is not an observed concurrent commit, so lock interactions on a real engine are unobserved: for example, whether the copy's later body read or the sweep's delete blocks on or conflicts with the rival's parent-bump row lock in a way that forces a redrive.
