title: A write the gate judged as a fresh create (add rung) can overwrite a rival's concurrently created file through catch_retry insert arbitration
description: DatabaseStorage.write gates every target in upsert mode before it stages anything. A path that is absent at the gate is judged only at the create rung (add). The ops.py ladder says add 'alters only one's own rows' and that overwriting anyone else's row needs contribute. If another principal (bob) commits a create of the same path inside the gate-to-apply window (the declared write:before-apply seam), alice's insert hits the unique (parent_id, name) index. On catch_retry engines (MSSQL, Oracle and the GENERIC floor used for unknown dialects), _resolve_rows probes the occupant, finds bob's non-directory row at the same path and, because overwrite defaults to True, calls staged.absorb. That turns alice's create into an unguarded clobbering update of bob's row. The update checks only entry_id, path and liveness, and no rights check runs again. Alice's body replaces bob's. owner_id stays bob's, and bob's earlier body goes to vfs_versions. When the same overwrite runs sequentially, it is refused with permission_denied. No isolation pin covers MSSQL, Oracle or GENERIC (op_isolation is None), so their statements run at the server default READ COMMITTED. Under READ COMMITTED each statement sees rows already committed. That holds for both MSSQL modes (locking and RCSI) and for Oracle's statement-level consistency, so the probe sees bob's committed row. The engines that are probably not affected are these. SQLite: BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock at alice's first read, so no rival can commit inside the window. PostgreSQL: the REPEATABLE READ pin makes ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE against a row the snapshot cannot see raise 40001, which is retryable; the whole method then runs again, and the gate judges the occupied path at contribute. MariaDB: the REPEATABLE READ snapshot hides bob's row from the probe, so it raises StaleSnapshot and the method runs again. I reproduced this myself on SQLite. I used the real write:before-apply seam and injected bob's create on alice's own session, the way a READ COMMITTED statement would observe it. Sequentially, alice was permission_denied. In the race, alice succeeded and both a system read and bob's own read returned 'ALICE'. That happened both on the native upsert path and with the profile forced to catch_retry. With overwrite=False, the race instead ended in vfs.exists. Impact: a peer who holds only add on a shared prefix can overwrite another principal's file, but only one that is being created at the same moment, at a path the attacker also targets. It is an integrity violation of one row and discloses nothing.
claimed_root_cause: WriteGate._decide authorizes a target that is absent at gate time only at the create rung (rights.py:884). Insert arbitration in writes.py then adopts a rival's row as the write target and never re-applies the primary-rung (contribute) check and owner floor that an occupied target needs. _resolve_rows absorbs a non-directory occupant under overwrite (writes.py:628-631), and _upsert_layer's on_conflict_do_update clobbers it (writes.py:489). The absorb arm of _update_materials (writes.py:690 onward) updates the row guarded only by path and liveness. The comment there calls this 'last-writer-wins between writes by design', but that design does not account for the different rungs the two writers hold.

trace.description: A lower-trust named subject (alice, holding add on /drop) calls write. gate.targets(..., 'upsert') judges the committed state, where the target path is absent.
An absent target passes when minting.reaches holds at the create rung (add). The primary rung (contribute) and the owner floor run only for paths that are occupied at gate time (rights.py:873-875).
The write:before-apply window. The snapshot read and staging are done and no mutation has run. A rival commit here goes unseen by the gate.
catch_retry profiles (MSSQL, Oracle, GENERIC) insert under a savepoint. The rival's committed row raises IntegrityError, and the chunk is redriven row by row in _resolve_rows.

The occupant probe, at READ COMMITTED, sees the rival's row at the same path. Because overwrite is True and the occupant is not a directory, staged.absorb(occupant.entry_id) retargets the create onto the rival's row. No rights check runs.

The absorb arm runs an unguarded update (entry_id, path, deleted_at IS NULL) of the rival's material columns. _replace_bodies then writes alice's body into bob's row, and mint_versions (writes.py:404) archives bob's replaced body.

evidence.description: write needs contribute on an occupied target and add on a fresh name. The ladder docstring (ops.py:117-121) says add alters only one's own rows and contribute overwrites anyone's.

MSSQL is catch_retry with no op_isolation pin, so the server default READ COMMITTED applies (RCSI also shows statements the committed rival row). ORACLE (dialects.py:529) and GENERIC (dialects.py:553) are the same.

PostgreSQL pins REPEATABLE READ, and 40001 is a retryable SQLSTATE (dialects.py:349). A clobbering ON CONFLICT against a row the snapshot cannot see should therefore run the method again rather than overwrite. MariaDB pins REPEATABLE READ (dialects.py:500), so its probe is snapshot-blinded and raises StaleSnapshot.
_CLOBBER_COLUMNS replace the material state and clear the tombstone, but leave out owner_id, so the overwritten row still records bob as its owner.
_execute_write runs gate and apply in one writer transaction with no row lock or serialization point on paths that are absent at gate time. Only SQLite gets BEGIN IMMEDIATE.

My own run on SQLite InMemoryStorage, injecting bob through the write:before-apply seam on alice's session. Sequential overwrite: permission_denied. Raced create: success=True, and both the system read and bob's read return 'ALICE'. The result is the same on the native upsert path and with arbitration forced to catch_retry. With overwrite=False the race ends in vfs.exists.

blockers: The decisive fact is engine concurrency: a genuine second transaction committing on MSSQL or Oracle (or a GENERIC-profile engine) inside alice's gate-to-apply window. Local execution is limited to SQLite. Production SQLite serializes writers with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so this race cannot happen there. Both the hunter's evidence and mine inject the rival on the victim's own session to stand in for READ COMMITTED visibility. That shows the code path and the missing re-authorization, but not observed engine behavior.

Whether PostgreSQL (REPEATABLE READ plus ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, expected to raise 40001) and MariaDB (snapshot-blinded probe, expected to raise StaleSnapshot) really run the method again and end with permission_denied, rather than overwriting, has not been observed on a real engine.

title: Caller-authored content_hash is stored unverified and keys cross-principal render lending
description: AsyncVirtualFileSystem.write(entries=[...]) stores the content_hash carried on a caller-built Entry without measuring the body storage holds. A bodiless bytes Entry (data=None, source='bytes') keeps any hash the caller names. This works with plain JSON-shaped model_validate dicts and needs no MEASURED_BODY context. The reindex render stage then lends a settled rendering per (content_hash, generation) from any row. The donor query has no owner, rights or deleted_at term. The landing guard compares the key only with the receiving row's own stored hash, which the attacker forged. Two cross-principal effects follow, and both reproduce locally. First, disclosure: a principal with no rights on another principal's file, who knows that file's sha-256, gets its rendered text in a row they own, readable through read and grep. A wrong guess stays pending, so the same write is an existence oracle. Second, integrity: a principal writes their own bytes, then overwrites the row bodiless under the hash of a known public document. The old blob stays, reindex renders the attacker's bytes, and the result is stamped under the forged hash. When another principal later uploads the real document, reindex serves them the attacker's text as their file's content, through read and grep. From source, the same trust also lets a contributor stop the version minting on overwrite (versions.py skips a pre-image whose hash equals the staged hash). The hunter reports that variant as executed; this verifier did not re-run it.
root_cause: write_rows (writes.py:163) passes entry.content_hash, entry.size_bytes and entry.lines from the caller's Entry into WritePlan.put_file, and _material_values (writes.py:1172) persists them. Entry._derive_and_measure (entry.py:232, 242) measures only when data is not None or source=='text', so a bodiless bytes Entry keeps the caller's hash. _replace_bodies (writes.py:987) skips a row with no content and no data, so a bodiless overwrite keeps the old blob under the new hash. No layer re-measures. render.py treats content_hash as proof of byte identity in two places: when cached_renderings picks a donor, and when land_renderings guards the stamp.
intended_behavior: A row's content_hash must always be the hash of the body storage holds for it. A content-kind write with neither content nor data must be refused, or must keep the stored row's measured metrics. Render dedup and version dedup must key only on hashes that storage measured itself. A tombstoned row must not lend its rendering.

Checks only that each item is an Entry, then path-gates and write-gates it. without_mount uses model_copy, which does not re-validate or re-measure.
Measures bytes only when data is not None, and text only when source=='text' (line 242). A source='bytes' Entry with data=None keeps the caller's content_hash and mime_type.
Passes entry.content_hash, size_bytes and lines unchanged into plan.put_file.
Writes the staged caller hash into the entry row. _replace_bodies (line 987) skips bodiless rows, so any earlier blob stays under the forged hash.
Selects the lowest-id settled donor per (content_hash, generation). Its predicates are hash, source, stamp and status only: no owner, rights or deleted_at term.
Reuses the cached or in-page rendering for any row whose (content_hash, generation) key matches, without reading that row's blob.
The stamp guard requires only that the receiving row's own content_hash equals the key. A forged hash passes, so the lent text is inserted as that row's content and is served by read, grep and glean.

evidence.description: The text branch measures with measure_text unless MEASURED_BODY is supplied. The bytes branch at line 232 runs only when data is not None. Nothing measures a bodiless bytes entry.
Only rows that have content or data count as bearing. A bodiless overwrite leaves the prior blob in place under the newly written hash.
The donor WHERE clause filters on hash membership, source, render_source_hash == content_hash, generation and settled status. It has no principal or deleted_at filter.
A pre-image version is skipped when its measured hash equals staged.content_hash, which is the caller's value.
A caller with list-level rights sees only path and kind, so the hash does not leak there. The attacker must learn H some other way, for example from a public or shared document.

In the reverse run, carol's upload of a public PDF is served dave's PLANTED text (cached=1).

Disclosure requires the attacker to know the exact sha-256 of the victim's bytes, for example a shared or leaked document. Poisoning requires the hash of a document the victim will later upload, such as a public form. It also requires the attacker's row to be the lowest-id settled donor for that hash, for example by planting first.
The operator runs reindex on the storage. This is routine: reindex is what produces any bytes rendering at all.

remediation.strategy: Measure at the storage seam. In write_rows, refuse a content-kind Entry that has neither content nor data, or ignore its metrics and keep the stored row's. Always compute content_hash, size_bytes and lines from the staged body in the storage layer, on the offload pool when the body is large, and never take them from the Entry. Make MEASURED_BODY router-internal, for example a private sentinel object rather than a public context key. Add entry.deleted_at IS NULL to the cached_renderings donor query. Once every hash is measured by storage, cross-row render lending is safe without a rights term.

title: edit's fuzzy replacers run quadratic pure-Python matching on the event loop inside the writer transaction, with no size, count or time bound
description: A principal that may modify one text entry, for example a file it just wrote itself, can send an edit whose old string does not match exactly. replace() then falls back to the fuzzy replacers in src/vfs/storage/replace.py. Three costs there grow with the square of the input. First, block_anchor_replacer scans forward from every first-anchor line to the end of the file when the last anchor never appears, which is O(L^2) in lines. Second, its similarity step runs a full-matrix pure-Python Levenshtein, which is O(M^2) in the length of the middle line. Third, line_trimmed_replacer recomputes each match's start offset with an O(i) sum, and replace() then computes a line number and splits the whole content again for every match when it builds the multi-match error, so L matches cost O(L^2). edit_rows calls this code synchronously inside the coroutine, once per target, inside the writer transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite). InMemoryStorage also serializes every session behind one asyncio.Lock. Nothing caps the length of old or new, the number of edits, the number of targets, or the wall time. So one small call freezes the host's shared event loop for every other agent in the process, and holds the mount's write lock the whole time. Every probe failed with vfs.invalid and committed nothing, so the attacker does not need a successful edit. Measured independently through the public verb: a 24 KB file with a 5-byte old string stalled the loop for 2.6 s (block_anchor). A 24 KB file with a 3-byte old string stalled it for 4.0 s (line_trimmed). A 4.8 KB request stalled it for 1.2 s (Levenshtein). Each doubling of input cost about 3.7x to 4.1x.
root_cause: replace() falls back to line_trimmed_replacer and block_anchor_replacer whenever the exact search misses. block_anchor_replacer's forward scan (replace.py:179-185) only stops when it finds the last anchor, so an absent last anchor makes it O(L^2). levenshtein (replace.py:61-82) builds a full O(n*m) Python matrix with no length cap, and calculate_similarity calls it for every middle line of every candidate. line_trimmed_replacer (replace.py:145) and replace()'s multi-match error builder (replace.py:321-325, which calls get_line_number and get_context_lines; the latter splits the whole content each time) recompute offsets and context for every match. edit_rows (writes.py:261) runs edited_entry inline in the async writer transaction for every target, with no call_offloaded, no deadline and no input caps. That differs from glean, indexing and signals, which do offload their CPU-bound work.
intended_behavior: An edit's matching cost should stay bounded: close to linear in the sizes of the content and of old. Fuzzy fallback should be refused, or capped, once it would exceed a declared work budget. CPU-bound matching should run off the event loop through call_offloaded with a deadline, the way the reindex, glean and signals paths already do. It should also run before the writer lock is taken, or at least not hold that lock for an unbounded time, so one caller cannot stall other principals sharing the host.

trace.description: The public verb takes caller-supplied path/observations plus old/new or an edits list. _gate_params (1031-1041) checks only types, then the call routes to storage at 1057.
old and new are typed 'str', edits is an EditOperation list and observations is a list. None has a length or count limit.
After the rung gate and the per-target modify check, edit_rows runs inside _execute_write (745). That is a writer transaction, opened BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite (1666-1673).
edited_entry runs synchronously in the coroutine for every target. A failed target appends an error and the loop continues to the next target.
apply_edits (replace.py:342-355) passes every EditOperation through replace().

An exact miss falls through to line_trimmed_replacer and then block_anchor_replacer. When there are many matches, 321-325 compute a line number and the context lines for each one, splitting the whole content every time.

When the last anchor is absent, the forward scan runs from each first-anchor line to the end of the file, O(L^2). calculate_similarity then calls levenshtein (202, defined 61-82), which is O(M^2) per middle line.

evidence.description: The nested loop over content_lines breaks only when the last anchor matches.
levenshtein allocates and fills a full (len(a)+1)x(len(b)+1) Python list matrix, with no length cap.
line_trimmed_replacer recomputes start_pos with an O(i) sum for every match.
get_context_lines splits the whole content and counts newlines in a prefix, once per match, while building the multi-match error.
edited_entry is called inline in the coroutine with no call_offloaded. Compare indexing.py:330, glean.py:872 and signals.py:123, which do offload.
_execute_write opens the writer transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite) and holds it across edit_rows.
The edit parameter specs declare no maximum for old, new, edits or observations.
On InMemoryStorage, _SerializedSessions puts every session behind one asyncio.Lock, so other principals' operations also queue behind the edit.

Phase 3 verifier's own sandboxed run through the public edit verb. Edit time grows about 4x per doubling for all three shapes. The longest event-loop gap equals the edit time. A control exact edit on a 16 KB file took 20 ms with a 3.5 ms gap.

Phase 5 verifier's independent sandboxed reproduction (script agents/f15-p5/artifacts/evidence/probe.py). On InMemoryStorage it reproduces the same three quadratic shapes: anchor 2.5 s, lev 1.1 s with 5764801 cells, trim 3.9-4.0 s at the largest size, loop gap equal to edit time. On file-backed SQLite DatabaseStorage, a separate connection's BEGIN IMMEDIATE (timeout 0) issued 150 ms into each longer edit was refused with 'database is locked', which confirms the writer lock is held across the matching.

conditions.description: The caller needs modify rights on at least one text entry, for example a file it wrote itself. No rights over other principals' data are needed.

The host process serves several agents or principals from one event loop and mount, which is the embedded-library model. The writer-lock effect applies to SQLite-backed mounts and to InMemoryStorage's serialized sessions. On other engines the event-loop stall remains. The host must also not impose its own cap on edit argument or file size; vfs itself has none.

The target's content and the old string are shaped to miss exactly and reach a quadratic fuzzy path. Three shapes work: many lines equal to the first anchor with the last anchor absent; one candidate whose long middle line differs; or many lines that match a whitespace-trimmed single-line old.

execution.attacker_perspective: A named principal (alice) has ordinary write and modify rights on her own file in a shared AsyncVirtualFileSystem over InMemoryStorage. Another principal (carol) reads her own file concurrently on the same loop.
payloads: write /t12000.txt content='a\n'*12000; edit(path='/t12000.txt', old='  a', new='z')
instructions: Run agents/f15-p5/artifacts/evidence/probe.py as tools/sandbox-run.py <scratch> ./.venv/bin/python -I <script>. The sandbox has no network, an empty environment, scratch-only writes, CPU 60 s, wall-clock 120 s and RSS 2 GiB.

For each shape, call the public edit verb at sizes n, 2n and 4n. Record the edit duration, the longest gap seen by a 2 ms asyncio ticker, the number of Levenshtein cells (counted by wrapping replace.levenshtein), and the latency of carol's concurrent read. A control exact-match edit gives the baseline.
execution.observed_result: Control exact edit on 16 KB: 20 ms, longest loop gap 3.5 ms. block_anchor at L=3000/6000/12000 lines: 176/642/2628 ms (x3.66, x4.09). levenshtein at M=600/1200/2400: 76/311/1214 ms (x4.09, x3.90), with Levenshtein cells 361201/1442401/5764801 (exactly quadratic). line_trimmed at L=3000/6000/12000: 266/1011/3995 ms (x3.81, x3.95). In every fuzzy probe the longest event-loop gap was within 15 ms of the edit duration. When carol's read was scheduled during the stall it waited the same span (2628 ms at anchor L=12000). Pure replace() alone reproduces the anchor timings (159/632/2552 ms). Every fuzzy edit returned vfs.invalid and committed nothing.

remediation.strategy:
Bound the work and move it off the event loop. (1) In block_anchor_replacer, precompute the indices of the stripped lines once, find each first anchor's next last anchor with bisect, and cap the number of candidates. That removes the O(L^2) scan. Compute line start offsets once with a prefix sum and use them in both fuzzy replacers. In replace(), compute line numbers from those offsets, split the content once, and list context for only the first few matches in the multi-match error. (2) Replace the Python levenshtein with a banded or early-exit version, or a vfs-core kernel. Skip fuzzy similarity when a middle line exceeds a declared length, or when len(content_lines)*len(find_lines) exceeds a work budget, and refuse with a classified invalid error that names the exact-match requirement. (3) Run the batch's edited_entry work through call_offloaded with a deadline, or do the matching before the writer transaction where the existing version guard keeps that safe. Regression test: count operations, never wall time. For example, count levenshtein cells or replacer loop iterations for the 'a
'*L / 'a
x
b' and '  a' shapes at L and 2L, and assert that growth is linear.

likelihood.reason: Any principal with modify rights on any one file, including its own, can trigger this with a request of a few KB plus a cheap prior write. Agents routinely send edits whose old string misses. Nothing in params.py, base.py or the storage caps old/new length, edit count, target count or file size, except MariaDB's packet cap on writes.

impact.reason: The stall freezes the shared event loop for every other principal on the host. On SQLite-backed mounts it also holds the writer lock, for a time that grows with the square of the input: 24 KB gave 2.6 to 4.0 s, and at the measured 4x per doubling about 100 KB would give roughly 40 to 60 s. The effect is transient: it ends when the call returns, leaves no persistent state, and the attacker can repeat it on every call. It costs availability only, with no confidentiality or integrity effect.

confidence.reason: The quadratic loops are plain in source and match the trace line for line. Two independent verifiers reproduced the result through the public verb in the sandbox. Growth was about 4x per doubling for all three shapes, the Levenshtein cell count was exactly quadratic, the loop stall equalled the edit time, a different principal's read was blocked, and on file-backed SQLite a rival connection's BEGIN IMMEDIATE was refused while the edit ran. A control exact edit stayed fast.

title: owner_id uses the engine's default collation on MariaDB, so a principal whose sub differs from another's only by case, accents or trailing spaces sees that owner's road directories
description: vfs compares principal identities exactly in Python: Principal.sub, grants.resolve and Rights.admits all use exact string equality. The SQL owner-arm predicate entry.owner_id == :owner runs on a column that gets a bytewise collation only on MSSQL. On MariaDB, owner_id compiles as a plain VARCHAR(255), so it inherits the database's default collation. path and name, by contrast, are pinned to VARBINARY there. MariaDB 11.8, the image the test leg uses, is expected to default to utf8mb4_uca1400_ai_ci, which ignores case and accents and pads trailing spaces; this was not observed in this audit. Principal.__post_init__ accepts subs such as 'ALICE', 'alice ' or 'Alicé'. Visibility.road asks SQL, through _owned_beneath, which hidden directories hold a row that each owner arm's sub owns, and Python never re-checks that answer. So a case-, accent- or space-variant principal is shown the victim's road directories in glob, ls and stat, including the trash view, and a write into such a directory fails as permission_denied instead of not_found. That reveals the names and existence of directories, which the principal could otherwise not see. File rows, content and grep results stay hidden, because the fetched rows pass Rights.admits/holds, which compare owner_id exactly. Grant and membership rows are re-keyed by exact sub in Python, so this does not escalate to inherited grants or groups. A second SQL-only consumer of the same predicate is the lexical aggregate in glean._visible_lexicon (glean.py:776, built from ranges.py:128-130). There the victim's chunks would also be counted into the BM25 corpus statistics. That is a minor statistical side channel, and it was not demonstrated. MySQL community is not a supported dialect per AGENTS.md and is served as GENERIC, but its DDL is the same VARCHAR. Postgres deterministic collations compare exactly and are not affected. Oracle is affected only under NLS_COMP=LINGUISTIC with a case-insensitive NLS_SORT. I reproduced this on SQLite, independently of the hunter, using a different tree (/hr/q3/alice-review.txt owned by 'alice', posture '/' none). With owner_id rewritten to COLLATE NOCASE, 'ALICE' sees /hr and /hr/q3 in glob and ls, stat('/hr/q3') succeeds, and its write into the directory returns permission_denied. With COLLATE RTRIM, 'alice ' sees the same. In both cases read is refused. The control 'bob' and the stock BINARY collation leak nothing (not_found).
claimed_root_cause: _string() (src/vfs/models/rows.py:179-188) adds a collation variant only for 'mssql'. On the mysql family (and Oracle under linguistic NLS settings), principal-bearing columns such as entries.owner_id (rows.py:471) and grants.principal_id are plain VARCHAR, and equality on them follows the server's collation. BytewiseString pins path and name to VARBINARY there (rows.py:224) but is not used for principal columns. The authority model treats subs as exact strings (grants.py:497, 629, 638-641). So the SQL-only owner predicates (rights.py:1250 in _owned_beneath for the road, and ranges.py:128-130 and rights.py:1220 for listing and aggregates) can admit rows that the Python authority would refuse. Where Python re-checks fetched rows (holds/admits), the gap closes. Where Python consumes the SQL result directly (the road directories, the lexicon aggregate), it leaks.

trace.description: The host builds Principal(sub) from its identity provider. Only empty or blank subs, '*', 'group:'-prefixed subs and the reserved names are refused, so 'ALICE', 'alice ' and 'Alicé' are accepted as principals distinct from 'alice'.
A named subject gets OwnerArm(sub, trimmed), keyed by its exact sub ('ALICE'), covering the mount outside its shared grants.

trace.scope: glob (also ls, stat and the trash view through the same road call)
trace.description: Directories the view does not show are passed to view.road(), and every path it returns is emitted as a road observation.
For each owner arm, _owned_beneath asks SQL which candidate directories hold a row owned by that owner. The result is added to the visible set with no Python re-check.
The predicate is row.c.owner_id == owner. Its equality follows the column's collation, so under a case-, accent- or pad-insensitive collation 'ALICE' or 'alice ' matches rows owned by 'alice'.

Column('owner_id', _string(255)) compiles to 'owner_id VARCHAR(255)' on mariadb/mysql, with no COLLATE and no binary type (confirmed by the hunter's DDL compile). Its comparisons therefore follow the server's default collation.

evidence.description: _string returns String(length).with_variant(String(length, collation=MSSQL_UTF8_COLLATION), 'mssql'). Only MSSQL gets a binary collation.
BytewiseString gives the mysql family VARBINARY(n) for path and name. Keys are pinned to bytewise comparison there; principal and owner columns are not.
Rights.admits does self._owned.get(owner_id), an exact dict lookup. This is why file rows stay hidden while road directories leak: the SQL and Python sides of the same rule disagree.

Grant rows are grouped by principal_id and looked up by exact sub and group name. Case-variant grant or membership rows that a collation-insensitive fetch returns are dropped in Python, so grant inheritance is not affected.
The narrow() docstring says fetched rows still pass holds() at the view's rung. That Python re-check covers listing rows but not road(), which returns SQL-derived directory paths directly.

_visible_lexicon aggregates count and sum(dl) in SQL over the visible-entries union, which uses owner_id == owner (ranges.py:128-130) with no row-level re-check. Under a case-insensitive collation it would count the victim's chunks into the corpus statistics. This is a minor side channel and was not demonstrated.

The MariaDB leg runs image mariadb:11.8 with no charset or collation override, and nothing in src sets mysql_collate or charset on the tables. The engine tests never use a case-variant principal, so no test pins this.

Independent SQLite simulation (sandboxed). Under BINARY, only 'alice' sees anything. Under NOCASE, 'ALICE' sees glob ['/hr','/hr/q3'] and ls /hr ['/hr/q3'], stat /hr/q3 succeeds, read is refused, and a write into the directory returns permission_denied. Under RTRIM, 'alice ' sees the same. 'bob' sees nothing and gets not_found throughout.

blockers: No real MariaDB or MySQL engine may run in this audit's sandbox (no Docker and no network, loopback included). The behavior was shown only on SQLite, with owner_id rewritten to COLLATE NOCASE or RTRIM as stand-ins for MariaDB's case-, accent- and pad-insensitive default collation. That MariaDB 11.8's actual default makes 'ALICE' = 'alice' and 'alice ' = 'alice' on the compiled column was not observed.

Whether a deployment exposes this depends on two facts outside source. The first is the production schema's database or table default collation. The second is whether the host's identity provider can issue a sub that differs from another principal's only by case, accents or trailing spaces.

On Oracle, the owner checks NLS_COMP and NLS_SORT for the session. The owner then confirms whether the identity provider or host mapping can mint subs that differ from existing ones only by case, accents or trailing spaces, for example user-chosen usernames or emails without normalisation.

title: Read-only PermissionMap overrides are bypassed by subtree verbs (delete, sweep, move, copy) addressed at a writable ancestor or destination
description: The router's PermissionMap is the per-prefix write policy enforced at the routing chokepoint before dispatch (README.md:127), and the mount-admin spec states that a map 'gates every path beneath'. The write gate resolves only the exact rel a verb addresses. A verb whose effect spans a subtree is checked against the rule that covers its addressed root, and never against a read-only override nested beneath that root. A non-system caller with ordinary row rights (the default fresh-mount posture) is refused on every direct write, edit, delete, sweep, move or copy inside the read-only region. Yet the same caller can: trash the read-only rows with delete(ancestor); purge them permanently with sweep(ancestor), after which restore finds nothing; move the ancestor out, rewrite the formerly read-only file at its new address, and move it back; or plant attacker content inside the read-only region in one call by copying or moving a staged tree onto an absent ancestor. The router already applies a subtree rule for bind sites (_busy_guard with subtree=True) but has no equivalent for permission overrides.
root_cause: check_writable (src/vfs/permissions.py:269-321) resolves the gated rel through PermissionMap._resolve. That function matches only overrides whose prefix equals or covers the path (permissions.py:196) and never looks at overrides lying strictly beneath it. _gate_entry (base.py:2902) calls check_writable_composed only for the addressed rels. It does this for every op, subtree-shaped ones included: single-path delete, restore and sweep at base.py:1748 and 2189, move's src and dest and copy's dest at base.py:2535. So a read rule deeper than the target is invisible to the gate.
intended_behavior: A read-only override must refuse every write-gated op whose effect lands at or beneath it. title: One refused embed batch at the head of the NULL-embedding keyset stops vector indexing for every later writer on the store
description: Each run of the reindex embed step starts again at chunk id 0. It selects the lowest-id rows that have no embedding, cuts them into batches using the provider's ceil(len/4) token estimate, and ends the whole step at the first page where any batch fails. When the provider refuses a batch deterministically, nothing splits the batch, skips it, or quarantines its rows. Those rows stay NULL and form the same head batch on every later run. The shipped OpenAI adapter meters batches with ceil(len/4) against 5/6 of its declared 300000-token request cap. Text denser than about 3.3 characters per real token, such as CJK, can therefore pass the estimate and still exceed the real cap. A principal with read_write on only its own subtree can write about 4096 small CJK files, about 2 MB in total. After that, no chunk written later by any principal on the same DatabaseStorage gets a vector, however many times reindex runs, and glean's vector leg misses that content. A smaller amount of such text leaves only the neighbouring rows in its batch unembedded, and limits the rest to one page of progress per run. Benign CJK corpora can trigger the same refusal.
root_cause: _embed_step (backend.py:1416) sets last = 0 on every run (1442). On any outcome.failure it records stopped_by and breaks out of the loop (1466-1468). It does not tell a deterministic refusal apart from a transient one, and it never advances past the failing page. embed_page (embed.py:319-325) keeps the first failure and lands only the batches that answered. _embed_with_retry (embed.py:346-355) retries only when the error carries Retry-After. No code bisects a refused batch, and there is no per-row failed state. So select_unembedded (embed.py:172-182) returns the same rows first on every run. token_batched (embed.py:112-133) meters each row with provider.estimate_tokens. For OpenAIEmbeddingProvider that is ceil(len/4) (openai.py:63-64, provider.py:96), checked against 5/6 of MAX_BATCH_TOKENS=300000 (openai.py:34, embed.py:121). Rows the writer controls can therefore make up a batch whose real token count exceeds the hard cap that the adapter itself declares.
intended_behavior: Batches should be metered with a bound that cannot undercount real tokens, for example the UTF-8 byte length for byte-level BPE. A batch refused without Retry-After should be bisected down to single rows. A single row that is still refused should be quarantined with a per-row failed state that select_unembedded and count_unembedded skip and that the report counts, as the render stage's _land already does (backend.py:1298-1321). The loop should keep advancing to later pages, so one writer's content cannot stop vector indexing for other principals.

trace.description: Principal alice writes ordinary CJK text files under /alice. Beyond the write gate, no rule limits their content, script or length. A write right on its own subtree is enough: with a closed root posture (posture='none') and read_write granted only on /alice, the same result follows.
Reindex chunks each body into rows of at most 2048 characters. Alice's rows get lower chunk ids than any chunk written after them.
Every run starts the keyset at last = 0.
The page is the lowest-id live rows whose embedding is NULL, so alice's rows come first on every run.

Each row's cost is provider.estimate_tokens, which is ceil(len/4) for the OpenAI adapter, checked against 250000 (5/6 of 300000). A batch of 2048 rows of 160 CJK characters estimates at 81920 tokens. With about 1 real token per ideograph it is 319488.
The provider refuses with a 400 that carries no Retry-After. The openai client does not retry a 400, and the error is re-raised without splitting the batch or marking its rows.
gather(return_exceptions=True) keeps the first failure. The refused batch's rows land nothing.
outcome.failure records stopped_by and breaks the loop, so later pages are never selected. The same rows head the next run, and every chunk written later by any principal stays with a NULL embedding.

evidence.description: A failed batch on any page breaks the whole embed loop (stopped_by at 1467, break at 1468).
last = 0 on every run, so the refused rows are always selected first again.
The sibling render stage retries row by row and quarantines a refused row as 'failed'. The embed step has nothing equivalent.
The batch budget is 5/6 of max_batch_tokens, metered by the provider's own estimate.
estimate_tokens is ceil(len/4), at least 1, whatever the script.
The shipped adapter declares MAX_BATCH_TOKENS=300000 and meters with the generic estimate_tokens (line 64).
_retry_after_seconds returns None for a 400 without Retry-After, so the refusal is re-raised without a split or a row mark.
The operator sees only a retryable 'unavailable' warning that names no rows, while reindex reports success=True.

Independent repro with the real OpenAIEmbeddingProvider and a real openai.BadRequestError. In both runs both requests were refused ([2048 inputs, 319488 tokens] each). Bob stayed at 1 of 41 chunks embedded, unembedded stayed 4136, success=True, and bob's glean vector leg returned hits=2.
Control without alice's files: bob was 41 of 41 embedded after run 1, and the vector leg returned hits=42.

Bob stayed at 1 of 41 embedded, unembedded=4136, success=True, and bob's vector leg returned hits=1. The control (f20-closed-control.json) had bob at 41 of 41 and hits=41.

Final-verifier rerun with the default posture and an independently written harness (f20_repro.py). 3 runs gave the same stop: bob at 1 of 41 embedded, unembedded 4136, vector hits=2. The control (f20-control.json) gave 41 of 41 and hits=42.

The proposed code change, the UTF-8 byte-length estimate patched onto the provider instance, under the same attack. One reindex embedded all 4136 rows in 9 requests, the largest at 83308 tokens, with unembedded=0 and no warning.

conditions.description: The mount uses an embedder whose hard caps are enforced on real tokens while vfs meters them with ceil(len/4). The shipped OpenAIEmbeddingProvider is the only shipped adapter that declares such caps. LangChain declares none, and the local providers do not refuse.

The token-dense rows must have lower chunk ids than the victims' unembedded rows: written before them, or still unembedded. A full stop needs about 4096 rows, one EMBED_PAGE_ROWS page, with more than about 147 real tokens per row. Fewer rows strand only the rows that share their batch, and limit progress to one page per run.

OpenAI's tokenizer must count the text at more than about 1.2 times len/4, and must refuse a request over 300000 tokens deterministically with a 400 and no Retry-After. The repository's adapter docstring declares this cap as documented. The installed openai client (_base_client.py _should_retry) retries only 408, 409, 429 and 5xx, not 400. The real cl100k token density of CJK was not measured locally; the repro used a stand-in counter of 1 token per ideograph.

execution.attacker_perspective: An agent or user (alice) that can write its own subtree of a shared DatabaseStorage mount using the OpenAI embedder. The fake client's embeddings.create counts 1 token per CJK ideograph and ceil(rest/4) for other text, and raises openai.BadRequestError with an httpx 400 response and no Retry-After when a request exceeds 300000 tokens.
As system, write /alice/README.txt and /bob/README.txt, grant each principal read_write on its own directory, and run reindex once.
As alice, write the 4096 CJK files. As bob, then write 40 ordinary English files.

Control: the same steps with zero alice files.

Bob stayed at 1 of 41 chunks embedded and unembedded=4136. reindex returned success=True with one warning, vfs.unavailable retryable=True: 'embedding stopped after 0 requests: BadRequestError: Requested 319488 tokens, max 300000 tokens per request'. remediation.strategy: Meter with a bound that cannot undercount, and stop treating a deterministic refusal as a reason to end the run. (1) The OpenAI adapter's estimate_tokens should return the UTF-8 byte length, because byte-level BPE never yields more tokens than bytes. (2) embed_page should bisect a batch refused without Retry-After, and return a single row that is still refused as a per-row failure. (3) Quarantine such rows with a failed marker that select_unembedded and count_unembedded exclude, reset it when the chunk's content_hash changes, and report the count in the embedding extra. (4) _embed_step should break only on transient failures (timeout, 429 or Retry-After, network errors) and otherwise keep advancing last. likelihood.reason: The attacker needs only ordinary write access to some path and about 2 MB of CJK text. The deployment must use the OpenAI embedder, the only shipped adapter with hard caps. Benign CJK or Cyrillic corpora with default 2048-character chunks also exceed the real cap, so this can happen without any malice.

impact.reason: The effect is persistent and store-wide, and it crosses principals: no chunk written later gets a vector on any reindex until an operator deletes or rewrites the offending rows or changes the code. glean's vector leg silently misses that content. The lexical leg and all other verbs are unaffected, and nothing is disclosed or lost. The warning names no rows and is marked retryable.

The one external fact, OpenAI's real CJK token density and its 400 on a request over 300000 tokens, rests on the repository's declared caps and public tokenizer behaviour, not on a local measurement. title: Markdown link extraction mints edges to rows the author cannot list, bypassing mkedge's target gate
description: Claim: a principal with write access to a markdown file (ann, contribute on /pub) can put a path she cannot list (/private/bob/plan.md) in a link. The operator's reindex resolves link targets against every live entry and inserts an extracted 'links' edge with no rights check, and mkedge would have refused the same edge as not_found. The edge then shows up in bob's inbound and neighborhood walks on his own private file, and bob cannot rmedge it. The mechanics reproduce. The security impact does not hold: no disclosure crosses a rights boundary, and nothing the access model protects is mutated.
claimed_root_cause: _resolve_candidates (src/vfs/storage/backends/database/links.py:149-165) maps candidate paths to entry ids with a plain SELECT filtered only by deleted_at IS NULL, with no Visibility for the source row's owner. publish_links (links.py:85-141) then inserts the edges through insert_arbitrated, inside the operator's reindex (backend.py:1377, indexing.py:338). mkedge, by contrast, needs list on the target (ops.py:157).

trace.description: ann, holding contribute on /pub, writes /pub/ann.md whose body links to /private/bob/plan.md, a path she cannot list. This is an authorized write of her own content.
The operator's reindex runs chunk_dirty.
The references of dirty markdown rows go to publish_links.
Candidate paths resolve against every live entry, with no rights filter.
An extracted links edge from ann's doc to bob's plan is inserted. The target row itself is not modified.
Every walk drops any edge whose far endpoint the viewer does not hold list on, so the edge is visible only to a principal who can list both ends.

evidence.description: The Needs docstring defines traverse as judging 'a row the verb reads without changing — a copy's source, an edge's target'. The ladder treats creating an edge as not changing its target. The target's list rung is a naming gate, not a write right over the target.

mkedge is Needs('contribute', traverse='list'): contribute on the source, list on the target. Any principal who can list bob's plan can author an inbound edge to it, and bob cannot rmedge it (rmedge needs contribute on the source, ops.py:158). So an unremovable inbound edge is the designed property of every edge, not something new here.

The record of the ladder's design (spec 165 / ADR 080) shows the edge rules exist to stop disclosure: 'rmedge leaks a hidden target today', a hidden target folded into the absent-target record, edges at list carry type only, traversal at list on both endpoints. No rule makes inbound-edge integrity a protected property of the target.

hop keeps a row only if view.holds(mapping, 'list') on the far endpoint, and walk.see records only the edges that pass. bob sees ann.md only because his posture (/ = read) already lets him read it. ann's outbound walk hides the target.

The unresolved and edge counts appear only in the operator's reindex Result. ann's write result and her walks carry nothing that tells a hidden target from an absent one, so the target gate's purpose (no existence oracle) holds.

Independent sandbox repro. ann's stat and mkedge to the plan return not_found at /private. After reindex (edges=1, unresolved=1, seen only by the operator), ann's outbound walk shows only her own doc. bob's inbound walk shows his plan plus /pub/ann.md, a file he can already read. bob's rmedge is refused permission_denied, exactly as it would be for an authored edge from any lister.

reason: Rejected on impact and declared intent; the mechanics are real. (1) The trace is accurate and reproduces: an extracted edge is minted to a target the author cannot list. (2) That gate exists to stop disclosure. In the ladder (ops.py:132) an edge's target is a row 'read without changing', and the spec 165 / ADR 080 record frames the edge rules as leak fixes. The extracted path preserves non-disclosure. ann gets no signal: her write succeeds whether or not the target exists, her walks hide the target, the edge context is never read back, and the unresolved count reaches only the operator. (3) No rights boundary is crossed for bob or anyone else. A walk passes an edge only when the viewer holds list on both ends. bob sees ann's doc only because he can already read it, and bob's plan row is not modified. (4) The 'unremovable' property is not new. Any inbound edge authored by a principal who can list the target is equally unremovable by bob, by design (rmedge needs contribute on the source). (5) What remains is a true derived index of ann's own authorized content: her document does link to that path, like a backlink. It puts content bob can already read next to his node. AI rule 1 asks for an unauthorized or unrequested action or a disclosure. Here no vfs action runs under bob's authority, and nothing is disclosed. Gate rule 5 excludes a gap with no affected principal or resource. At most this is a consistency hardening note: extracted edges could follow mkedge's target rule for uniformity. A separate concern, not judged here: with an opt-in Ranker centrality signal (signals.py, min-max scaled whole-corpus), extracted edges to hidden targets might move glean priors that ann can observe. That needs non-default configuration and is a different root cause; it would need its own candidate.

title: Uncapped grant rows naming another principal grow that principal's glean statement fan and event-loop stalls
description: Any principal that holds read_write at some path can write any number of grant rows that name another sub or a group: id. It does this at distinct sub-paths it controls, and those paths need not hold a row. Every later glean by the grantee compiles all of those rows. The glean vector leg then runs one statement per visibility clause, and there is about one clause per 100 planted prefixes. Rows planted only through the public grant() verb reproduced this on InMemoryStorage (SQLite). At 0, 400 and 1600 rows the victim's warm glean issued 10, 14 and 26 statements over 1, 5 and 17 clauses. Its time rose from about 8 ms to 0.7-1.0 s, and the largest event-loop gap rose from 1 ms to 149-178 ms. glob stayed at 4 statements. Under a restrictive posture (none at the root, mallory holding read_write only on its own subtree) the victim cannot revoke the rows: the call returns permission_denied. Under the default read_write root posture, anonymous can plant the rows, but the victim (or anyone) can also revoke them. Each further grant also retires the grantee's RightsCache entry, which forces a fresh compile whose cost grows with n.
root_cause: grant_rows and _grant_refusal check only that the principal is lawful, that the level is grantable, and that the granter holds read_write at the path. Nothing bounds how many rows may name a principal other than the granter. The glean vector leg (_vector_leg, glean.py:648-649) always takes view.clauses() and runs one statement per clause. It does not use the single-statement range-source join that Visibility.narrow uses through visible_entries. So the number of statements per victim call grows linearly with the pieces another principal plants in the victim's rights. Resolution.compile and the building of each statement run on the event loop.
intended_behavior: A grantee's per-call cost should not grow without bound because of rows another principal plants. One fix keeps the vector leg's visibility pushdown at a constant statement count, as narrow() already does through visible_entries. Another bounds the rows that may name a principal, or requires the grantee's consent before such rows count.

trace.description: Public grant verb. Any caller with read_write at the path may name any lawful principal (another sub or a group: id).
_grant_refusal checks lawfulness, level and read_write at the path, with no count bound. Line 918 stamp_principals then retires the grantee's cached compile.
On a cache miss it reads every grant row naming the grantee's subjects and groups, then compiles them in Python with Resolution.compile.
Splits the rights into OR-clauses of at most arm_budget (200) units, so the clause count grows linearly with the planted prefixes.
Takes view.clauses() and, at line 649, builds one statement per clause. Each probe window executes all of them, so the number of statements per call grows with the grantee's piece count.

evidence.description: _lawful_principal accepts any non-reserved, non-blank id within the column length. The grant path has no row-count check.
The default posture is read_write at the root, so under defaults anonymous passes the grant gate. Under that posture the victim can also revoke (observed).

narrow() uses the single-statement visible_entries join where the dialect declares a range_source, and falls back to the per-clause fan otherwise (the GENERIC floor). glean's vector leg does not take this path.
arm_budget caps clause width at 200 arms. Each statement stays bounded while the number of statements grows.

title: glean's link-centrality prior is built from hidden rows, so a partial caller's visible scores reveal hidden in-links
description: When an operator declares a link signal (InDegree, PageRank or Katz) on a DatabaseStorage Ranker, reindex computes one prior over the whole corpus. It counts every live entry and every non-fs edge, including edges authored on rows and markdown links extracted from bodies the eventual reader cannot see. At query time glean multiplies each visible candidate's fused score by the stored factor whatever the caller's view, then min-max scales. A partial caller (a named principal without whole-mount read, or anonymous) therefore gets glean scores that differ between two worlds that differ only in hidden rows. With a visible calibrator file of known in-degree, the caller can tell whether, and roughly how many, hidden entries reference a visible file, while graph inbound, glob and read on the same data correctly reveal nothing. The same path lets a writer use files only they can see as an invisible link farm that raises a readable target in every other principal's ranking.
root_cause: signals.collect_graph (src/vfs/storage/backends/database/signals.py:72-118) takes no authority or Visibility and pages every live entry and every non-reserved edge. DatabaseStorage._signal_phase calls it once per reindex (backend.py:1332) and the Rust centrality kernel (models/signals.py:28-61) scores over that whole graph, smooths through directories and min-max scales over all files. signal_factors (signals.py:194-263) takes no view, and glean_rows applies its factors to every candidate after both visibility-filtered legs (glean.py:390-392). The visible-set treatment glean gives N, mean length and df is never applied to the signal leg.
intended_behavior: glean_rows' own docstring states that under a partial view the statistics are the visible set's, 'so a hidden row never moves a visible score' (glean.py:249-251). The permission-ladder research says degree counts and stored link signals must count only edges whose both endpoints the caller can list (context/research/2026-10-14-the-permission-ladder-list-and-contribute.md:98). The statistics-under-permissions memo names this exact leak and asks for visible-set treatment or a documented exemption (context/research/2026-09-28-search-statistics-under-permissions-precedent.md:349). Spec 136, which landed the signals, has no exemption. The earlier-generation archived spec 009 invariant 6 also says centrality must be computed over the visible subgraph only.

trace.description: A partial or anonymous caller issues glean(query, globs=..., authority=...). The router routes the call to the mount with that authority, and the storage resolves it to a partial Visibility.
Earlier, reindex collected the graph once with no authority or view, then computed and published each declared signal.
Every non-fs edge between live entries is collected, including edges from rows hidden from the eventual reader and links extracted from hidden markdown bodies.
The Rust kernel computes the measure over the full graph, applies hierarchy smoothing that includes hidden files, and min-max scales over all files.
Stored values for the candidates become 1 + beta*t(v) multipliers. The function has no view parameter.
Each visible entry's fused score is multiplied by the factor that hidden rows influenced, then ordered, min-max scaled and returned to the partial caller as Observation.score.

evidence.description: The docstring promises that under a partial view 'a hidden row never moves a visible score'.
signal_factors is called with no view, after both legs and the overlay have filtered rows through the view.
collect_graph has no authority or view parameter. It pages every live entry and every non-reserved edge.
The comparable control the signal leg lacks: graph hops keep a row only if view.holds(mapping, 'list'), so hidden in-links are left out of graph inbound.
Stated rule: degree counts and stored link signals must count only edges with both endpoints at list or above for the caller.
Names the leak ('A visible file's centrality can reveal hidden in-links') and requires visible-set treatment or a documented exemption. Neither exists.
The default Ranker declares no signals, so the leak needs an operator to opt in to a link signal.

Verifier's own sandboxed run. bob's and anonymous's glean scores change with k hidden alice edges or hidden markdown links. The no-signal control is unchanged by k. graph, glob and read reveal nothing about /alice.

conditions.description: The operator declares a link signal (InDegree, PageRank or Katz, for example Signal('centrality', weight=0.5)) on the DatabaseStorage Ranker. The default Ranker declares none.

reindex has run since the hidden edges or hidden link-bearing bodies were written. Hidden rows reference a visible file. The caller can read that file and, for counting, a calibrator file with a known visible in-degree that matches the same query.

The reader is any named or anonymous principal without whole-mount read (a partial Visibility). For the steering variant, the writer needs modify on their own hidden files and read on the target, which is what mkedge requires.

execution.attacker_perspective: bob, or anonymous, can read /pub but not /alice. Comparing glean scores, he learns whether, and roughly how many, of alice's private files reference /pub/a.md. Separately, alice can raise /pub/a.md in everyone's ranking through links from files only she can see.
payloads: system writes /pub/a.md 'zebra report alpha', /pub/b.md 'zebra report gamma', /pub/c.md 'zebra report delta with many more filler words here', /alice/n0..n4.md; posture / none; posture /pub read; grant alice read_write on /alice; mkedge /pub/c.md -> /pub/b.md (visible calibrator)
edge variant: alice mkedge /alice/n{i}.md -> /pub/a.md for i < k; markdown variant: /alice/n{i}.md bodies contain '[x](/pub/a.md)' for i < k, no mkedge
instructions: Ran agents/v22-p3/scratch/verify_prior.py under tools/sandbox-run.py (no network, empty env, scratch-only writes, CPU 60 s, wall 120 s, RSS 2 GiB) with ./.venv/bin/python -I. SQLite files in scratch only.

For k in {0,1,3}, in both the edge and markdown variants, recorded bob's and anonymous's glean scores, legs.signals, graph inbound on /kb/pub/a.md, glob /kb/alice/**, and read /kb/alice/n0.md. As a control, ran the edge variant with k=0 and k=3 using a default Ranker with no signals.
execution.observed_result: bob and anonymous get identical scores. a.md/b.md: k=0 0.6875/1.0; k=1 1.0/1.0; k=3 1.0/0.848484848. The markdown-body variant gives exactly the same values. With no signal declared, scores are 1.0/1.0 for both k=0 and k=3, which isolates the change to the signal leg. In every world, bob's and anonymous's graph inbound on a.md lists no /alice row, glob /kb/alice/** is empty, and read /kb/alice/n0.md fails. legs.signals reports centrality applied.

remediation.strategy: Never apply a whole-corpus prior to a partial caller. Smallest fix: in glean_rows, call signal_factors only when view is None. Under a partial view, skip the signal leg and emit a fixed explain that looks the same whether or not any edges exist, so 'applied' and 'no entry earned a value' stop leaking. The fuller design computes or stores priors per visibility class, for example over the rows everyone may read, or computes a visible-subgraph prior at query time, counting only edges whose both endpoints the caller can list. Regression test: two worlds that differ only in hidden edges or hidden link-bearing bodies must give a partial caller byte-identical glean observations and legs.signals.

likelihood.reason: An operator must opt in to a link signal on the Ranker (the default declares none), and reindex must run after the hidden links exist. Once both hold, any partial or anonymous reader can query repeatedly with no special rights.

impact.reason: It discloses link metadata of hidden rows: whether, and roughly how many, hidden entries reference a visible file, including references extracted from hidden bodies. It does not disclose bodies or paths. It also allows invisible ranking manipulation, but only of documents the victim can already read.

confidence.reason: Every source step was verified, and no visibility parameter exists anywhere on the signal path. The code's own docstring and the project's permission research state the opposite policy. An independent sandboxed two-world run shows partial callers' scores moving with hidden edges and hidden markdown links, while a no-signal control is unchanged and graph, glob and read reveal nothing.

title: Posture writes and relabels rely on bytewise path comparison that Oracle and GENERIC dialects do not pin
description: Row rights trust the everyone_level label stored on each row (Rights.admits, grants.py:491). A posture change does two things in SQL alone, with no Python re-check of which rows were hit. It writes the everyone posture row (_upsert_grant, matching on path_prefix = P). It also relabels the subtree (relabel_spans / _relabel_opens, matching on lo < path < hi). The gate in front of them, _grant_refusal, works out reach at P bytewise in Python. BytewiseString pins a bytewise collation only on postgresql, mssql and the mysql family. Oracle and every unknown dialect served from GENERIC get a plain String with no pin, so their comparisons follow whatever the engine defaults to. Suppose such an engine compares paths case- or accent-insensitively, for example Oracle with NLS_COMP=LINGUISTIC and a _CI or _AI NLS_SORT, a non-binary DEFAULT_COLLATION, or a GENERIC engine whose default collation is case-insensitive. Then a caller who holds read_write at /Projects through an open parent posture can call posture('/Projects', 'read'). That call rewrites the labels, and the everyone posture row, of another owner's binary-distinct private subtree /projects. Any third user can then read that owner's private rows. The caller would be refused at /projects itself. I reproduced this mechanism locally in a SQLite analogue: path columns were forced to COLLATE NOCASE by patching BytewiseString in-process. Under stock bytewise collation, the same steps leave the row hidden. That this happens on a real Oracle or GENERIC deployment is not yet observed.
claimed_root_cause: BytewiseString.load_dialect_impl pins a bytewise collation only for postgresql, mssql and the mysql family. Oracle and GENERIC fall through to plain String (rows.py:229), and the docstring at rows.py:208-212 accepts that as an ordering and byte-budget degradation that rests on Oracle's NLS_SORT=BINARY default. Two security-relevant writers decide in SQL alone which rows they change: the posture upsert key (rights.py:1375) and the relabel range and point UPDATEs (labels.py:351, 356, 503-504). Both depend on bytewise comparison. The rights.py module docstring (lines 45-49) says every engine compares bytewise, but nothing pins or checks that on Oracle or GENERIC.

trace.description: A named lower-trust caller asks for a posture at path P (for example /Projects). The call goes through _grant_write into set_posture.

posture_rows fetches the chain's posture rows through a SQL IN-list. label_of (line 1328) and reaches() then judge P bytewise in Python, so a case-variant posture row at /projects does not change the label at /Projects, and the gate passes on the parent's open posture.

UPDATE grants WHERE principal_id = '*' AND path_prefix = P, with path_prefix itself in the SET values. Under a non-binary comparison this can match and rewrite another owner's case-variant posture row.
The planned spans for P go to relabel_spans, which runs point UPDATEs by membership (line 351) and open-range UPDATEs through _relabel_opens (line 356).

UPDATE entries SET everyone_level = rank WHERE OR(path > lo AND path < hi). No Python check follows. A non-binary comparison widens the match to rows outside P's binary region, and Rights.admits (grants.py:491) then trusts the new label.

evidence.description: The fallback for Oracle and unknown dialects is a plain String with no collation pin. Lines 208-212 call this an accepted degradation that relies on the engine default (NLS_SORT=BINARY).
grants.path_prefix is a BytewiseString, so the posture key gets the same unpinned type on Oracle and GENERIC.
The module contract, lines 45-49, says each bound goes through the path column's type 'so every engine compares bytewise'. Nothing enforces that on Oracle or GENERIC.
The posture upsert key compares path_prefix in SQL only, and the UPDATE also overwrites path_prefix.

The literal-OR relabel UPDATE. It runs for Oracle (range_source json_table_clob is not a branch _relabel_opens handles) and for the GENERIC floor (no range_source). No Python check of which rows it touched follows.
Rights.admits accepts any row whose stored everyone_level meets the needed rung, unless the row lies in a hole.

The GENERIC floor declares no session settings and has no collation knowledge, and profile_for serves every unknown dialect from it. The ORACLE profile also declares no session_settings, so no ALTER SESSION pins NLS_COMP or NLS_SORT. By contrast, SQLite pins case_sensitive_like at line 400.

Verifier-run SQLite analogue in the sandbox, with the script in agents/v23-p3/artifacts/evidence/analogue.py. Setup: root posture read_write, bob writes /projects/secret.md and sets /projects to none. ann's posture at /projects is refused (not_found). ann's posture at /Projects succeeds. In stock mode carol's read of /projects/secret.md stays not_found. In nocase mode it succeeds and returns 'bob private'. This is an analogue only: column-level NOCASE also makes SQLite's unique indexes case-insensitive, which is not how Oracle's session-level linguistic comparison behaves.

blockers: Whether any supported Oracle deployment runs with NLS_COMP=LINGUISTIC and a case- or accent-insensitive NLS_SORT (set through init parameters, logon triggers or NLS_LANG), or with a non-binary schema or column DEFAULT_COLLATION. The Oracle default (NLS_COMP=BINARY) compares bytewise and is not affected. Real engines and Docker are prohibited in this run, so this cannot be observed.
Which NLS settings python-oracledb sessions (thin and thick) inherit at vfs's connection setup. The ORACLE profile issues no ALTER SESSION, and the inherited values are not visible in source.

Which SQLAlchemy dialects a host would actually serve through the GENERIC floor, and whether their default path collation is case-insensitive (MySQL community, for example, defaults to utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci but is in the mysql family that gets VARBINARY; other unknown engines are outside source).

The local demonstration is a SQLite COLLATE NOCASE analogue, not Oracle or a GENERIC engine. It shows that vfs adds no bytewise guard after the SQL writers, but it does not show that a real deployment compares non-bytewise.

validation_plan.local: Owner-run, in the db_test skill's Oracle Docker leg. Open the storage's sessions with ALTER SESSION SET NLS_COMP=LINGUISTIC NLS_SORT=BINARY_CI, through a test-only connect hook. As system, set posture '/' to read_write. As bob, write /projects/secret.md and set posture /projects to none. Confirm that carol's read is not_found and that ann's posture at /projects is refused. As ann, set posture /Projects to read. Then check (a) whether the grants row ('*', '/projects') was rewritten or renamed, (b) the everyone_level on /projects/secret.md, and (c) whether carol's read succeeds. Repeat with stock NLS (BINARY) as the control. My SQLite analogue script (agents/v23-p3/artifacts/evidence/analogue.py) gives the exact step sequence.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should confirm which NLS_COMP, NLS_SORT and DEFAULT_COLLATION values are supported for Oracle mounts, and whether unknown dialects are expected to compare bytewise. Suggested fixes: pin bytewise comparison on Oracle (COLLATE BINARY on the path, name and path_prefix columns, or ALTER SESSION SET NLS_COMP=BINARY NLS_SORT=BINARY in ORACLE.session_settings). At connect time, probe GENERIC engines with a case-variant comparison and refuse any that are not bytewise. As defence in depth, re-check in Python that the posture-row key and the relabelled rows fall inside P's binary region.

title: grep and glean count rows the caller cannot read toward their budgets, so the warnings and row counts reveal hidden rows and, through the gram index, what they contain
description: Take a caller with partial rights in DatabaseStorage or InMemoryStorage, such as a named user granted read on one prefix. For that caller, grep and glean work out whether a call hit its candidate or overlay budget from candidate rows that have not yet passed the per-row Visibility check. Hidden rows therefore use up budget slots and then get dropped. That has two visible effects. First, a truncated warning appears or disappears. Second, a matching row the caller can see goes missing from the results. Both change with rows the caller cannot see, even though a direct read of those rows answers not_found. There are three variants, all reproduced at the shipped budgets. (1) grep scan tier, used for unindexed rows or allow_scan: any hidden unindexed row in scope that sorts before the visible rows triggers the 'candidate budget' warning and drops one visible match. (2) grep index tier: whether a hidden indexed row contains the searched literal changes the row count (25,000 vs 24,999) and the warning text. That is a content oracle on rows the caller cannot read. (3) glean overlay: one hidden unindexed row triggers the 'overlay budget' warning and drops one visible hit, at a threshold of only 500 rows.
root_cause: In grep_rows, the index side caps doc_ids at CANDIDATE_BUDGET and sets nominated_count from the posting kernel (grep.py:243-254). The scan side gets its overflow flag from entries_for_scan, which runs SELECT ... ORDER BY path LIMIT limit+1 with no visibility predicate (scope.py:279-294). The per-row view.holds filter runs only afterwards (grep.py:261, 303; glean.py:380). So hidden rows take budget slots and set the truncation flags (grep.py:254, 269, 299; glean.py:384) before they are thrown away. The rights module says a statement with a LIMIT should carry the visibility pushdown (rights.py:38-39), and that hidden rows should read as absent. entries_for_scan and the nomination kernel do neither.
intended_behavior: For a caller with partial rights, every grep and glean output (rows, row count, truncation records) should depend only on rows the caller's Visibility admits. A hidden row should affect search output exactly as a row that does not exist. The rights module states this: hidden reads exactly as absent, a road directory reveals nothing beyond the visible rows' own paths, and SQL statements with a LIMIT carry the visibility pushdown.

trace.description: A named or anonymous caller with partial rights calls grep. The backend resolves a partial Visibility through _viewed and passes it to grep_rows as view.

The index tier gets candidate doc ids and nominated_count from the posting kernel over every indexed row in scope, hidden rows included. The ids are capped at CANDIDATE_BUDGET before any visibility check.
The 'candidate budget' truncation is recorded from nominated_count, which includes hidden rows.
view.holds drops hidden rows only after they have used candidate slots. remaining (line 269) is then computed from the visible rows that survived.
The scan and overlay fetch is SELECT ... ORDER BY path LIMIT limit+1 with no visibility predicate. Hidden rows fill the window, and overflow is set from the unfiltered count (scope.py:281, 294).
The scan-side overflow, which includes hidden rows, adds the 'candidate budget' truncation. view.holds at line 303 then removes the hidden rows that displaced visible ones.
The glean overlay applies view.holds after entries_for_scan(limit=OVERLAY_BUDGET=500). At line 384 it records 'overlay budget' from the overflow flag, which includes hidden rows.
The truncation records built from those counts, and the shortened row list, are returned to the partial caller as warning errors on the Result.

evidence.description: The grep_rows docstring admits that the candidate budget still counts hidden candidates. The behaviour is known, but it is not treated as a disclosure, and no other layer compensates for it.
CANDIDATE_BUDGET is 25,000, the threshold at which grep's index and scan variants flip.
OVERLAY_BUDGET is 500, a much lower threshold for the glean variant.
The unscoped scan statement orders by path and limits to limit+1 with no visibility pushdown, so hidden rows that sort earlier take the window.
The stated design is that SQL predicates are pushdowns that narrow toward the Visibility wherever a statement's shape needs one, a LIMIT included. entries_for_scan has a LIMIT and no such pushdown.
The stated policy is that hidden reads exactly as absent. The search budgets break this for derived search outputs.

Observed at the real budget of 25,000, scan tier. No hidden row: 25,000 rows, no warning. One hidden row, either content: 24,999 rows and a 'candidate budget' truncated warning. Direct read of the hidden row: not_found.

Observed at the real budget of 25,000, index tier after reindex. No hidden row, or a hidden row without 'needle': 25,000 rows and the 'overlay not consulted' warning. Hidden row containing 'needle': 24,999 rows and the plain 'candidate budget' warning. This is a content oracle on an unreadable row.
Observed at the real OVERLAY_BUDGET of 500. No hidden row: 500 rows, no warning. One hidden unindexed row: 499 rows and an 'overlay budget' truncated warning.

The grep reproduction script. It sets posture none at /, grants alice read on /pub, and as system writes N visible '/pub' files plus an optional hidden '/aaa-sec/h.txt'. It then compares alice's grep output.
The glean reproduction script, using the same world shape with 500 visible unindexed files.

conditions.description: The attacker is a named, group, or anonymous principal with partial rights: read on some prefixes and no rights on the target prefix. A system caller is not affected.

The grep variants need about 25,000 visible entries in the call's scope that match the pattern on the index tier, or are unindexed on the scan tier. The glean variant needs 500 visible unindexed entries. The attacker can create these with add or write rights on any prefix in the same mount, or an existing visible corpus can supply them. Globs let the attacker scope the call to its own prefix plus the target prefix.

Ordering decides which rows are displaced. On the scan tier and the glean overlay, hidden rows must sort by path before the window's visible rows, and the attacker chooses its own path names. On the index tier, the hidden row's doc id must fall inside the first CANDIDATE_BUDGET ids. The scan and overlay variants also need the hidden rows to be unindexed, that is before reindex publishes them.

execution.attacker_perspective: Alice holds read only on /pub (root posture none). She is not allowed to learn whether rows exist under /aaa-sec, or what they contain. A direct read of /aaa-sec/h.txt answers not_found.
instructions: Create an InMemoryStorage and call first_touch. As Authority.system(), set posture('/', 'none') and grant alice 'read' on /pub.

As system, optionally write a hidden /aaa-sec/h.txt, in one world containing 'needle secret' and in another 'other text'. Then write 25,000 visible /pub/vNNNNNN.txt files containing 'needle visible'. For the index tier, call reindex().
As alice, call grep(pattern='needle', output_mode='files', allow_scan=True). Record the row count and the truncated warnings. Confirm that read('/aaa-sec/h.txt') as alice returns not_found.
For glean, write 500 visible unindexed /pub files containing 'lantern', with and without one hidden /aaa-sec row. Call glean(query='lantern') as alice and compare.

Run everything under tools/sandbox-run.py with the repo .venv python -I. The scripts are agents/v24-p3/artifacts/evidence/repro_grep.py (args: 25000 scan, or 25000 index none|without|with) and repro_glean.py.
execution.observed_result: All runs used the unpatched shipped budgets. Scan tier: 25,000 rows and no warning without a hidden row; 24,999 rows and a 'candidate budget' truncated warning with one hidden row of any content. Index tier: 25,000 rows and the 'overlay not consulted' warning when no hidden row matches; 24,999 rows and the plain 'candidate budget' warning when the hidden row contains 'needle'. Glean: 500 rows and no warning, against 499 rows and an 'overlay budget' warning when one hidden row is present. In every world, alice's direct read of the hidden row answered not_found.

remediation.strategy: Apply the caller's Visibility before counting anything toward a budget. In entries_for_scan, add the visibility_clauses / visible_entries pushdown to the WHERE clause, so LIMIT limit+1 and overflow count only rows the caller may see. Thread view into entries_for_scan from grep_rows and glean_rows. On the index tier, restrict the allow-list or the kernel's candidate ids to visible entries before the CANDIDATE_BUDGET cap and the nominated_count comparison. This could be done by computing allow_list_ids under the view pushdown, or by filtering doc ids through the view before capping. Replace the grep_rows docstring note that the budget counts hidden candidates with a regression test. The test should assert that grep and glean output (rows and truncation records) is identical for a partial caller whether or not hidden rows are present, both just below and at each budget.

likelihood.reason: The attacker needs partial rights plus about 25,000 matching or unindexed visible entries in scope for grep, or 500 unindexed entries for glean. Typically that means add rights to create padding. Ordering conditions also apply. Each query yields about one bit.

impact.reason: This is a one-bit-per-query oracle across the row-rights boundary. It reveals whether hidden rows exist in a scope, and on the index tier whether a hidden row contains the searched grams, which can be repeated to probe content. It also silently drops visible matches. It does not read hidden bodies or paths directly.

confidence.reason: The path is fully visible in the source, including the docstring that admits the behaviour. All three variants were reproduced locally under the sandbox at the shipped CANDIDATE_BUDGET of 25,000 and OVERLAY_BUDGET of 500, with a not_found direct-read control on the same row.
